subtopic: Frequency table with an unknown frequency
statement: A test of four questions is marked out of 4 for a class. The frequency of each value is given below (value: frequency): 1: 1; 2: k; 3: 3; 4: 2. The mean of the data is $\frac{5}{2}$. (a) Find the value of $k$. [3] (b) Find the variance of the data. [3]
markscheme: (a) total frequency $=k + 6$ [M1] $\sum fx=2 k + 18$, and $\dfrac{\sum fx}{\sum f}=\frac{5}{2}$ gives $2 k + 18=\frac{5}{2}(k + 6)$ [M1] $k=6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sum fx^2=84$ and $n=12$ [M1] variance $=\dfrac{\sum fx^2}{n}-\bar x^2$ [M1] $=\frac{3}{4}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write the total frequency in terms of $k$ first, then use mean $=\sum fx/\sum f$ to form an equation. Variance is the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean.

subtopic: Frequency table with an unknown frequency
statement: Students in a school club recorded the number of books they read in a month. The frequency of each value is given below (value: frequency): 0: 3; 1: k; 2: 5; 3: 3. The mean of the data is $\frac{3}{2}$. (a) Find the value of $k$. [3] (b) Find the variance of the data. [3]
markscheme: (a) total frequency $=k + 11$ [M1] $\sum fx=k + 19$, and $\dfrac{\sum fx}{\sum f}=\frac{3}{2}$ gives $k + 19=\frac{3}{2}(k + 11)$ [M1] $k=5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sum fx^2=52$ and $n=16$ [M1] variance $=\dfrac{\sum fx^2}{n}-\bar x^2$ [M1] $=1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write the total frequency in terms of $k$ first, then use mean $=\sum fx/\sum f$ to form an equation. Variance is the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean.

subtopic: Frequency table with an unknown frequency
statement: A shop records the number of items per customer basket. The frequency of each value is given below (value: frequency): 2: 2; 4: k; 6: 6; 8: 1. The mean of the data is $5$. (a) Find the value of $k$. [3] (b) Find the variance of the data. [3]
markscheme: (a) total frequency $=k + 9$ [M1] $\sum fx=4 k + 48$, and $\dfrac{\sum fx}{\sum f}=5$ gives $4 k + 48=5(k + 9)$ [M1] $k=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sum fx^2=336$ and $n=12$ [M1] variance $=\dfrac{\sum fx^2}{n}-\bar x^2$ [M1] $=3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write the total frequency in terms of $k$ first, then use mean $=\sum fx/\sum f$ to form an equation. Variance is the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean.

subtopic: Effect of a linear change on summary statistics
statement: The times, in minutes, taken by a group of runners were recorded. The mean is $12$ and the standard deviation is $3$. (a) Each value $x$ is replaced by $y=2x+5$. Write down the mean and the standard deviation of $y$. [2] (b) Find $\sum y^2$ given that there are $n=10$ values. [3]
markscheme: (a) mean $=2\times12+5=29$ [A1] standard deviation $=2\times3=6$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) variance of $y$ $=36$ [M1] $\dfrac{\sum y^2}{10}-29^2=36$ [M1] $\sum y^2=8770$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A linear change $y=ax+b$ changes the mean to $a\bar x+b$ and the standard deviation to $|a|s$; the shift $b$ does not affect the spread.

subtopic: Effect of a linear change on summary statistics
statement: The marks of a group of students in a test were recorded. The mean is $40$ and the standard deviation is $5$. (a) Each value $x$ is replaced by $y=-3x+10$. Write down the mean and the standard deviation of $y$. [2] (b) Find $\sum y^2$ given that there are $n=20$ values. [3]
markscheme: (a) mean $=-3\times40+10=-110$ [A1] standard deviation $=3\times5=15$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) variance of $y$ $=225$ [M1] $\dfrac{\sum y^2}{20}--110^2=225$ [M1] $\sum y^2=246500$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A linear change $y=ax+b$ changes the mean to $a\bar x+b$ and the standard deviation to $|a|s$; the shift $b$ does not affect the spread.

subtopic: Effect of a linear change on summary statistics
statement: The lengths, in cm, of some seedlings were measured. The mean is $8$ and the standard deviation is $1.5$. (a) Each value $x$ is replaced by $y=4x-6$. Write down the mean and the standard deviation of $y$. [2] (b) Find $\sum y^2$ given that there are $n=15$ values. [3]
markscheme: (a) mean $=4\times8-6=26$ [A1] standard deviation $=4\times1.5=6.0$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) variance of $y$ $=36.0$ [M1] $\dfrac{\sum y^2}{15}-26^2=36.0$ [M1] $\sum y^2=10680.0$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A linear change $y=ax+b$ changes the mean to $a\bar x+b$ and the standard deviation to $|a|s$; the shift $b$ does not affect the spread.

subtopic: Mean and standard deviation from grouped data
statement: The ages of the customers at a café one morning were recorded. The grouped data are (class: frequency) $0\le x<10$: 5; $10\le x<20$: 12; $20\le x<30$: 18; $30\le x<40$: 5. (a) Write down the modal class. [1] (b) Use the midpoints of the classes to estimate the mean and the standard deviation. [3] (c) Estimate the median by linear interpolation. [3]
markscheme: (a) $20\le x<30$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) midpoints $5, 15, 25, 35$ [M1] mean $\approx20.8$ [A1] standard deviation $\approx8.63$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) total frequency $40$ so median is the $20$th value [M1] the cumulative frequency reaches this in the class containing it, interpolate within that class [M1] median $\approx21.7$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Replace each class by its midpoint and enter the midpoints and frequencies as a list on your calculator. For the median, interpolate inside the class where the cumulative frequency passes $n/2$.

subtopic: Outliers using the 1.5 x IQR rule
statement: The number of emails received in ten days by an office was recorded. The data, in increasing order, are $3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 30$. (a) Find the median and the lower and upper quartiles. [3] (b) Find the interquartile range. [1] (c) Determine, showing your working, whether the data contain any outliers. [3]
markscheme: (a) median $=8.5$ [A1] $Q_1=6$ [A1] $Q_3=11$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $IQR=11-6=5$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) upper fence $=11+1.5\times5=18.5$ [M1] lower fence $=6-1.5\times5=-1.5$ [A1] $30$ lies outside the fences, so it is an outlier [R1] [3 marks]
tips: An outlier is a value more than $1.5\times IQR$ below $Q_1$ or above $Q_3$. Compute both fences before comparing.

subtopic: Outliers using the 1.5 x IQR rule
statement: The scores of nine competitors in a quiz were recorded. The data, in increasing order, are $1, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19$. (a) Find the median and the lower and upper quartiles. [3] (b) Find the interquartile range. [1] (c) Determine, showing your working, whether the data contain any outliers. [3]
markscheme: (a) median $=15$ [A1] $Q_1=12.5$ [A1] $Q_3=17.5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $IQR=17.5-12.5=5$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) upper fence $=17.5+1.5\times5=25$ [M1] lower fence $=12.5-1.5\times5=5$ [A1] $1$ lies outside the fences, so it is an outlier [R1] [3 marks]
tips: An outlier is a value more than $1.5\times IQR$ below $Q_1$ or above $Q_3$. Compute both fences before comparing.

subtopic: Outliers using the 1.5 x IQR rule
statement: The delivery times, in minutes, of twelve orders were recorded. The data, in increasing order, are $20, 22, 23, 25, 26, 27, 28, 30, 31, 32, 33, 60$. (a) Find the median and the lower and upper quartiles. [3] (b) Find the interquartile range. [1] (c) Determine, showing your working, whether the data contain any outliers. [3]
markscheme: (a) median $=27.5$ [A1] $Q_1=24$ [A1] $Q_3=31.5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $IQR=31.5-24=7.5$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) upper fence $=31.5+1.5\times7.5=42.75$ [M1] lower fence $=24-1.5\times7.5=12.75$ [A1] $60$ lies outside the fences, so it is an outlier [R1] [3 marks]
tips: An outlier is a value more than $1.5\times IQR$ below $Q_1$ or above $Q_3$. Compute both fences before comparing.

subtopic: Combining the mean and standard deviation of two groups
statement: Two classes sat the same test. Group A has $10$ values with mean $5$ and variance $4$. Group B has $10$ values with mean $9$ and variance $4$. (a) Find the mean of all the values combined. [2] (b) Find the variance of all the values combined. [4]
tips: Variances cannot be averaged directly. Recover $\sum x^2$ for each group using $\sum x^2=n(\sigma^2+\bar x^2)$, add, then subtract the square of the combined mean.

subtopic: Combining the mean and standard deviation of two groups
statement: Two machines each filled bags of flour; the masses of the bags, in grams above a target, were recorded. Group A has $20$ values with mean $12$ and variance $9$. Group B has $30$ values with mean $17$ and variance $16$. (a) Find the mean of all the values combined. [2] (b) Find the variance of all the values combined. [4]
tips: Variances cannot be averaged directly. Recover $\sum x^2$ for each group using $\sum x^2=n(\sigma^2+\bar x^2)$, add, then subtract the square of the combined mean.

subtopic: Correcting a recorded data set
statement: A teacher records the scores of $30$ students in a test. The mean is calculated as $62$ and the standard deviation as $8$. Later it is found that one score of $45$ was wrongly recorded and should have been $54$. (a) Find the correct mean. [2] (b) Find the correct standard deviation. [4]
tips: Rebuild $\sum x$ and $\sum x^2$ from the stated mean and standard deviation, fix the two sums, then recompute.

subtopic: Cumulative frequency, median and quartiles
statement: A survey recorded the time, in minutes, that 60 students spent on homework one evening. The cumulative frequencies are (upper class boundary: cumulative frequency) $<10$: 8; $<20$: 28; $<30$: 48; $<40$: 60, and the lowest value is 0. (a) State the number of observations and the position of the median. [2] (b) Use linear interpolation to estimate the median. [3] (c) Estimate the interquartile range. [3]
markscheme: (a) $n=60$ [A1] median at the $30$th value [A1] [2 marks] (b) median lies in class $20$ to $30$ [A1] $\dfrac{30-28}{20}\times10$ [M1] median $=21$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $Q_1=13.5$ [A1] $Q_3=28.5$ [A1] $IQR=15$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: On a cumulative frequency curve, the median is the value at $n/2$, the quartiles at $n/4$ and $3n/4$. Interpolate linearly inside the class where the cumulative frequency passes the target.

subtopic: Cumulative frequency, median and quartiles
statement: A cycling club recorded the distances, in km, ridden by 80 members in a month. The cumulative frequencies are (upper class boundary: cumulative frequency) $<20$: 10; $<40$: 30; $<60$: 70; $<80$: 80, and the lowest value is 0. (a) State the number of observations and the position of the median. [2] (b) Use linear interpolation to estimate the median. [3] (c) Estimate the interquartile range. [3]
markscheme: (a) $n=80$ [A1] median at the $40$th value [A1] [2 marks] (b) median lies in class $40$ to $60$ [A1] $\dfrac{40-30}{40}\times20$ [M1] median $=45$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $Q_1=30$ [A1] $Q_3=55$ [A1] $IQR=25$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: On a cumulative frequency curve, the median is the value at $n/2$, the quartiles at $n/4$ and $3n/4$. Interpolate linearly inside the class where the cumulative frequency passes the target.

subtopic: Stratified sampling
statement: A school wants to survey students about its canteen. The population has 400 members split into groups: Year 10 (150), Year 11 (120), Year 12 (130). A stratified sample of size $40$ is to be taken. (a) Find the number of members that should be sampled from each group. [3] (b) State one advantage of stratified sampling over simple random sampling. [1]
markscheme: (a) Year 10: $\dfrac{150}{400}\times40=15$ [A1] Year 11: $\dfrac{120}{400}\times40=12$ [A1] Year 12: $\dfrac{130}{400}\times40=13$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) the sample reflects the proportions of the groups in the population, so each group is represented [R1] [1 mark]
tips: In stratified sampling the sample size from each stratum is proportional to its size in the population.

subtopic: Stratified sampling
statement: A researcher surveys businesses in a region. The population has 400 members split into groups: small firms (240), medium firms (100), large firms (60). A stratified sample of size $20$ is to be taken. (a) Find the number of members that should be sampled from each group. [3] (b) State one advantage of stratified sampling over simple random sampling. [1]
markscheme: (a) small firms: $\dfrac{240}{400}\times20=12$ [A1] medium firms: $\dfrac{100}{400}\times20=5$ [A1] large firms: $\dfrac{60}{400}\times20=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) the sample reflects the proportions of the groups in the population, so each group is represented [R1] [1 mark]
tips: In stratified sampling the sample size from each stratum is proportional to its size in the population.

subtopic: Effect of adding an observation on mean and standard deviation
statement: The ages of members of a book club were recorded. A set of $24$ values has mean $52$ and standard deviation $6$. A further value $70$ is added to the set. (a) Find the new mean. [2] (b) Find the new standard deviation. [3] (c) State, with a reason, whether the standard deviation increases or decreases when a value equal to the mean $52$ is added instead. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\sum x=24\times52=1248.0$ [M1] new mean $=\dfrac{1318.0}{25}=52.72$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\sum x^2=24(6^2+52^2)=65760.0$ [M1] new $\sum x^2=70660.0$ [A1] $\sigma=\sqrt{\dfrac{70660.0}{25}-52.72^2}=6.86$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) a value equal to the mean adds nothing to $\sum(x-\bar x)^2$ but increases $n$ [R1] so the variance, and hence the standard deviation, decreases [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Reconstruct $\sum x$ and $\sum x^2$ from the mean and standard deviation, update both sums, then recompute. A new value at the mean leaves the sum of squared deviations unchanged while $n$ grows.

subtopic: Effect of adding an observation on mean and standard deviation
statement: The masses, in kg, of fifteen parcels were recorded. A set of $15$ values has mean $3.2$ and standard deviation $0.8$. A further value $5.6$ is added to the set. (a) Find the new mean. [2] (b) Find the new standard deviation. [3] (c) State, with a reason, whether the standard deviation increases or decreases when a value equal to the mean $3.2$ is added instead. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\sum x=15\times3.2=48.000$ [M1] new mean $=\dfrac{53.600}{16}=3.350$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\sum x^2=15(0.8^2+3.2^2)=163.200$ [M1] new $\sum x^2=194.560$ [A1] $\sigma=\sqrt{\dfrac{194.560}{16}-3.350^2}=0.968$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) a value equal to the mean adds nothing to $\sum(x-\bar x)^2$ but increases $n$ [R1] so the variance, and hence the standard deviation, decreases [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Reconstruct $\sum x$ and $\sum x^2$ from the mean and standard deviation, update both sums, then recompute. A new value at the mean leaves the sum of squared deviations unchanged while $n$ grows.

subtopic: Effect of removing an outlier on mean and standard deviation
statement: The daily sales, in thousands of dollars, of a shop were recorded over $21$ days. The mean was $8.5$ and the standard deviation was $2.1$. The sales of $15$ thousand on one exceptional day are then excluded from the data. (a) Find the mean of the remaining sales. [2] (b) Find the standard deviation of the remaining sales. [3]
tips: Rebuild the sums from the summary statistics, subtract the excluded value (and its square), and divide by the new count.

subtopic: Box plot interpretation from summary values
statement: The times, in minutes, taken by 80 commuters to reach work were recorded. The five-number summary of $80$ values is minimum $4$, lower quartile $10$, median $14$, upper quartile $19$, maximum $40$. (a) Find the range and the interquartile range. [2] (b) Approximately how many of the $80$ values are greater than $19$? [1] (c) Determine whether the maximum value is an outlier. [3]
markscheme: (a) range $=40-4=36$ [A1] $IQR=19-10=9$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) about a quarter of the values, so about $20$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) upper fence $=19+1.5\times9=32.5$ [M1][A1] 40 is greater than the fence, so it is an outlier [R1] [3 marks]
tips: A quarter of the data lies above the upper quartile. The outlier test compares the extreme value with $Q_3+1.5\times IQR$.

subtopic: Box plot interpretation from summary values
statement: The scores of 120 players in a game were recorded. The five-number summary of $120$ values is minimum $12$, lower quartile $35$, median $41$, upper quartile $52$, maximum $70$. (a) Find the range and the interquartile range. [2] (b) Approximately how many of the $120$ values are greater than $52$? [1] (c) Determine whether the maximum value is an outlier. [3]
markscheme: (a) range $=70-12=58$ [A1] $IQR=52-35=17$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) about a quarter of the values, so about $30$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) upper fence $=52+1.5\times17=77.5$ [M1][A1] 70 is not greater than the fence, so it is not an outlier [R1] [3 marks]
tips: A quarter of the data lies above the upper quartile. The outlier test compares the extreme value with $Q_3+1.5\times IQR$.

subtopic: Quartiles and standard deviation from a frequency table
statement: The numbers of goals scored in each of 40 matches were recorded. The frequency table is (value: frequency) 0: 4; 1: 9; 2: 12; 3: 8; 4: 5; 5: 2. (a) Find the mean and the standard deviation. [3] (b) Find the median and the interquartile range. [3]
markscheme: (a) enter values and frequencies [M1] mean $=2.175$ [A1] standard deviation $=1.32$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) median $=2$ [A1] $Q_1=1$, $Q_3=3$ [A1] $IQR=2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the one-variable statistics function with a frequency list. Quartiles come from the cumulative frequencies.

subtopic: Binomial probabilities with a calculator
statement: Each seed planted in a nursery germinates with probability $0.4$, independently of the others. Fifteen seeds are planted. Let $X$ be the number of successes, so that $X\sim B(15,0.4)$. (a) Find $P(X=6)$. [2] (b) Find $P(X\le4)$. [2] (c) Find $P(X\ge9)$. [2] (d) Find the mean and the standard deviation of $X$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $P(X=6)=\binom{15}{6}0.4^{6}(1-0.4)^{9}$ [M1] $=0.207$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(X\le4)$ using binomial cdf [M1] $=0.217$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(X\ge9)=1-P(X\le8)$ [M1] $=0.0950$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) mean $=15\times0.4=6.000$ [A1] standard deviation $=\sqrt{15\times0.4\times0.6000}=1.90$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: State $X\sim B(n,p)$ and use the binomial pdf and cdf functions. For 'at least', use the complement of the cdf.

subtopic: Binomial probabilities with a calculator

(a) Find $P(X=3)$. [2] (b) Find $P(X\le2)$. [2] (c) Find $P(X\ge5)$. [2] (d) Find the mean and the standard deviation of $X$. [2]
tips: State $X\sim B(n,p)$ and use the binomial pdf and cdf functions. For 'at least', use the complement of the cdf.

subtopic: Binomial probabilities with a calculator
statement: A basketball player scores a free throw with probability $0.7$ each time, independently. She takes 12 free throws. Let $X$ be the number of successes, so that $X\sim B(12,0.7)$. (a) Find $P(X=9)$. [2] (b) Find $P(X\le7)$. [2] (c) Find $P(X\ge11)$. [2] (d) Find the mean and the standard deviation of $X$. [2]
tips: State $X\sim B(n,p)$ and use the binomial pdf and cdf functions. For 'at least', use the complement of the cdf.

subtopic: Binomial: finding the smallest n
statement: A call center connects a call successfully with probability $0.08$ each time a number is dialed. Let $X$ be the number of successes in $n$ independent trials, each with probability of success $0.08$. (a) Write down the probability that there is at least one success, in terms of $n$. [2] (b) Find the smallest value of $n$ for which $P(X\ge1)>0.95$. [4]
tips: Use the complement: at least one success is $1-P(X=0)$. When dividing by $\ln$ of a number less than 1, remember the inequality reverses.

subtopic: Binomial: finding the smallest n
statement: A fisherman catches a fish with probability $0.2$ each time he casts his line. Let $X$ be the number of successes in $n$ independent trials, each with probability of success $0.2$. (a) Write down the probability that there is at least one success, in terms of $n$. [2] (b) Find the smallest value of $n$ for which $P(X\ge1)>0.99$. [4]
tips: Use the complement: at least one success is $1-P(X=0)$. When dividing by $\ln$ of a number less than 1, remember the inequality reverses.

subtopic: Binomial distribution with exact answers
statement: A spinner lands on red with the stated probability on each spin. Let $X$ be the number of successes in $4$ independent trials, where the probability of success on each trial is $\frac{1}{3}$. (a) Find $P(X=2)$ giving your answer as a fraction. [2] (b) Find $P(X\le1)$. [3] (c) Find $E(X)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\binom{4}{2}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{2}$ [M1] $=\frac{8}{27}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(X=0)=\frac{16}{81}$ [A1] $P(X=1)=\frac{32}{81}$ [A1] $P(X\le1)=\frac{16}{27}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $E(X)=\frac{4}{3}$ [A1] $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{8}{9}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Write each probability as $\binom{n}{r}p^r(1-p)^{n-r}$ and keep fractions exact. $E(X)=np$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=np(1-p)$.

subtopic: Binomial distribution with exact answers
statement: A student guesses the answers to a short quiz. Let $X$ be the number of successes in $5$ independent trials, where the probability of success on each trial is $\frac{1}{5}$. (a) Find $P(X=2)$ giving your answer as a fraction. [2] (b) Find $P(X\le1)$. [3] (c) Find $E(X)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [2]
tips: Write each probability as $\binom{n}{r}p^r(1-p)^{n-r}$ and keep fractions exact. $E(X)=np$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=np(1-p)$.

subtopic: Normal probabilities and percentiles
statement: The masses of bags of rice filled by a machine are recorded. The quantity $X$ is normally distributed with mean $500$ g and standard deviation $12$ g. (a) Find $P(X<490)$. [1] (b) Find $P(490<X<520)$. [2] (c) Find the value $q$ such that $P(X<q)=0.9$. [2] (d) Find the probability that a value is more than 520 g, given that it is more than 490 g. [3]
markscheme: (a) $P(X<490)=0.202$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) normal cdf between the limits [M1] $=0.750$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $q$ from inverse normal [M1] $q=515.4$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $P(X>520\mid X>490)=\dfrac{P(X>520)}{P(X>490)}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{0.04779}{0.7977}$ [A1] $=0.0599$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Define the normal distribution on your calculator, then use cdf for probabilities and inverse normal for percentiles. A conditional probability with $X>b$ inside $X>a$ is a ratio of two tail areas.

subtopic: Normal probabilities and percentiles
statement: The heights of adult men in a town are modeled. The quantity $X$ is normally distributed with mean $172$ cm and standard deviation $8$ cm. (a) Find $P(X<165)$. [1] (b) Find $P(165<X<185)$. [2] (c) Find the value $q$ such that $P(X<q)=0.95$. [2] (d) Find the probability that a value is more than 185 cm, given that it is more than 165 cm. [3]
markscheme: (a) $P(X<165)=0.191$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) normal cdf between the limits [M1] $=0.757$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $q$ from inverse normal [M1] $q=185.2$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $P(X>185\mid X>165)=\dfrac{P(X>185)}{P(X>165)}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{0.05208}{0.8092}$ [A1] $=0.0644$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Define the normal distribution on your calculator, then use cdf for probabilities and inverse normal for percentiles. A conditional probability with $X>b$ inside $X>a$ is a ratio of two tail areas.

subtopic: Normal probabilities and percentiles
statement: The time taken by customers to complete an online form is modeled. The quantity $X$ is normally distributed with mean $45$ seconds and standard deviation $6$ seconds. (a) Find $P(X<40)$. [1] (b) Find $P(40<X<55)$. [2] (c) Find the value $q$ such that $P(X<q)=0.25$. [2] (d) Find the probability that a value is more than 55 seconds, given that it is more than 40 seconds. [3]
markscheme: (a) $P(X<40)=0.202$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) normal cdf between the limits [M1] $=0.750$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $q$ from inverse normal [M1] $q=40.95$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $P(X>55\mid X>40)=\dfrac{P(X>55)}{P(X>40)}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{0.04779}{0.7977}$ [A1] $=0.0599$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Define the normal distribution on your calculator, then use cdf for probabilities and inverse normal for percentiles. A conditional probability with $X>b$ inside $X>a$ is a ratio of two tail areas.

subtopic: Finding the mean and standard deviation of a normal variable from two probabilities
statement: The lifetimes, in days, of a type of battery are modeled. Let $X$ be normally distributed with $P(X<70)=0.2023$ and $P(X<95)=0.8944$. (a) Write down two equations connecting $\mu$ and $\sigma$. [3] (b) Hence find $\mu$ and $\sigma$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{70-\mu}{\sigma}=-0.8334$ [M1][A1] $\dfrac{95-\mu}{\sigma}=1.250$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) subtract the equations [M1] $\sigma=12.0$ [A1] $\mu=80.0$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Convert each probability to a $z$-value with inverse normal, then solve the two linear equations in $\mu$ and $\sigma$.

subtopic: Finding the mean and standard deviation of a normal variable from two probabilities
statement: The lengths of time, in minutes, taken by trains on a route are modeled. Let $X$ be normally distributed with $P(X<30)=0.2119$ and $P(X<41)=0.9192$. (a) Write down two equations connecting $\mu$ and $\sigma$. [3] (b) Hence find $\mu$ and $\sigma$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{30-\mu}{\sigma}=-0.7998$ [M1][A1] $\dfrac{41-\mu}{\sigma}=1.400$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) subtract the equations [M1] $\sigma=5.00$ [A1] $\mu=34.0$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Convert each probability to a $z$-value with inverse normal, then solve the two linear equations in $\mu$ and $\sigma$.

subtopic: Normal distribution: symmetry and conditional probability without a calculator
statement: The random variable $X$ is normally distributed with mean $50$ and $P(X>58)=0.1$. (a) Write down $P(X<42)$. [1] (b) Find $P(42<X<58)$. [2] (c) Find $P(X<58\mid X>50)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) symmetry about the mean $50$: $42$ and $58$ are equally far from $50$ [A1] so $P(X<42)=0.1$ [1 mark] (b) $P(42<X<58)=1-0.1-0.1$ [M1] $=0.8$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(50<X<58)=0.5-0.1=0.4$ [M1][A1] $P(X>50)=0.5$ so conditional probability $=\dfrac{0.4}{0.5}=0.8$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use symmetry about the mean to turn tail areas into each other, and draw the bell curve with the regions shaded.

subtopic: Normal distribution: symmetry and conditional probability without a calculator
statement: The mass $M$ kg of a parcel is normally distributed with mean $40$ and $P(M<30)=0.15$. (a) Find $P(M>50)$. [1] (b) Find $P(30<M<50)$. [2] (c) Find $P(M<40\mid M<50)$. [3]
tips: A conditional probability $P(A\mid B)$ with $A\subset B$ is $P(A)/P(B)$. Use symmetry to read off the tail probabilities.

subtopic: Discrete random variable: unknown probabilities, mean and variance
statement: A fair-looking game assigns scores to a spinner. The probability distribution of a discrete random variable $X$ is given by $P(X=x)=kx$ for $x=1,2,3,4$, where $k$ is a constant. (a) Find the value of $k$. [2] (b) Find $P(X\ge3)$. [1] (c) Find $E(X)$. [2] (d) Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sum P(X=x)=1$ [M1] gives $k=\frac{1}{10}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(X\ge3)=P(3)+P(4)=\frac{7}{10}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $E(X)=\sum xP(X=x)$ [M1] $=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $E(X^2)=10$ [A1] $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$ [M1] $=1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The probabilities must sum to $1$. Use $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$.

subtopic: Discrete random variable: unknown probabilities, mean and variance
statement: A school lottery awards a score $X$ to each ticket. The probability distribution of a discrete random variable $X$ is given by $P(X=x)=k(5-x)$ for $x=1,2,3,4$, where $k$ is a constant. (a) Find the value of $k$. [2] (b) Find $P(X\ge3)$. [1] (c) Find $E(X)$. [2] (d) Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sum P(X=x)=1$ [M1] gives $k=\frac{1}{10}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(X\ge3)=P(3)+P(4)=\frac{3}{10}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $E(X)=\sum xP(X=x)$ [M1] $=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $E(X^2)=5$ [A1] $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$ [M1] $=1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The probabilities must sum to $1$. Use $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$.

subtopic: Discrete random variable: unknown probabilities, mean and variance
statement: The number of attempts $X$ needed by a trainee to pass a task has the following distribution. The probability distribution of a discrete random variable $X$ is given by $P(X=x)=\dfrac{k}{x}$ for $x=1,2,3,4$, where $k$ is a constant. (a) Find the value of $k$. [2] (b) Find $P(X\ge3)$. [1] (c) Find $E(X)$. [2] (d) Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [3]
tips: The probabilities must sum to $1$. Use $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$.

subtopic: Continuous random variable with a quadratic pdf
statement: The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)=kx^2$ for $0\le x\le3$, and $f(x)=0$ otherwise. (a) Find the value of $k$. [2] (b) Find $E(X)$. [2] (c) Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [3] (d) Find the exact value of the median. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\int_0^3kx^2\,dx=1$ [M1] $9k=1$ so $k=\frac{1}{9}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^3x\cdot\frac{1}{9}x^2\,dx$ [M1] $=\frac{9}{4}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $E(X^2)=\displaystyle\int_0^3\frac{1}{9}x^4\,dx=\frac{27}{5}$ [M1][A1] $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{27}{5}-\left(\frac{9}{4}\right)^2=\frac{27}{80}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\displaystyle\int_0^m\frac{1}{9}x^2\,dx=\dfrac12$ [M1] $\dfrac{m^3}{27}=\dfrac12$ [A1] $m=\frac{3 \cdot 2^{\frac{2}{3}}}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Integrate the pdf over its support to find $k$. The median $m$ satisfies $\int_{\text{lower}}^{m}f(x)\,dx=\tfrac12$.

subtopic: Continuous random variable with a piecewise linear pdf
statement: The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)=\begin{cases}kx & 0\le x\le2\\ k(4-x) & 2<x\le4\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$ where $k$ is a constant. (a) Find the value of $k$ by sketching the graph of $f$ or by integration. [3] (b) Write down the mode and, by symmetry, the mean of $X$. [2] (c) Find $P(X\le1)$. [2] (d) Find $P(1<X<3)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) the graph is a triangle with base $4$ and height $2k$ [M1] area $=\dfrac12\times4\times2k=1$ [M1] $k=\dfrac14$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) mode $=2$ [A1] the graph is symmetric about $x=2$ so $E(X)=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac x4\,dx$ [M1] $=\dfrac18$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) by symmetry $P(X\ge3)=P(X\le1)=\dfrac18$ [M1][A1] $P(1<X<3)=1-\dfrac18-\dfrac18=\dfrac34$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: When a pdf is piecewise linear, areas are often easiest as triangles. The mean of a symmetric distribution lies on its axis of symmetry.

subtopic: Continuous random variable with an exponential pdf
statement: The time $T$ minutes spent waiting for a bus has probability density function $f(t)=ke^{-t/4}$ for $t\ge0$, and $f(t)=0$ otherwise. (a) Show that $k=\dfrac14$. [3] (b) Find $P(T>6)$. [2] (c) Find $E(T)$. [2] (d) Find the median waiting time. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty ke^{-t/4}\,dt=1$ [M1] $\left[-4ke^{-t/4}\right]_0^\infty=4k$ [A1] $4k=1$ so $k=\dfrac14$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_6^\infty\dfrac14e^{-t/4}\,dt=e^{-1.5}$ [M1] $=0.223$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty \dfrac t4e^{-t/4}\,dt$ [M1] $=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\displaystyle\int_0^m\dfrac14e^{-t/4}\,dt=\dfrac12$ gives $1-e^{-m/4}=\dfrac12$ [M1][A1] $m=4\ln2=2.77$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The area under $f$ must equal $1$. Use integration (or your calculator) over $[0,\infty)$; the median satisfies $P(T\le m)=0.5$.

subtopic: Continuous random variable with a trigonometric pdf
statement: The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)=k\sin x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$, and $f(x)=0$ otherwise. (a) Find the value of $k$. [2] (b) Find $P\left(X<\dfrac\pi3\right)$. [2] (c) Use your calculator to find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\int_0^\pi k\sin x\,dx=1$ [M1] $2k=1$ so $k=\dfrac12$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/3}\dfrac12\sin x\,dx=\dfrac14$ [M1] [A1] [2 marks] (c) $E(X)=\displaystyle\int_0^\pi\tfrac12x\sin x\,dx=\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] $E(X^2)=2.935$ [A1] $\operatorname{Var}(X)=0.467$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use $\int_0^\pi\sin x\,dx=2$ to find $k$. Variance is $E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$; the integrals can be evaluated numerically.

subtopic: Normal then binomial
statement: The volume $V$ ml of juice in a carton is normally distributed with mean $250$ and standard deviation $6$. A carton is underfilled if it contains less than $240$ ml. (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen carton is underfilled. [2] (b) A box contains 10 randomly chosen cartons. Find the probability that at least one is underfilled. [3] (c) Find the expected number of boxes, out of 200 such boxes, that contain at least one underfilled carton. [2]
tips: First find the probability of a single success using the normal distribution, then use it as the parameter $p$ of a binomial model.

subtopic: Expected value and fair price of a game
statement: In a game at a fair, a player rolls a special die. With probability $\frac12$ nothing is won, with probability $\frac3{10}$ the player wins $\$2$ and with probability $\frac15$ the player wins $\$10$. (a) Find the expected gain of a player per game (the prize minus the stake of $\$3$). [3] (b) Find the stake that would make the game fair. [1]
markscheme: (a) expected prize $=\sum\text{prize}\times\text{probability}$ [M1] $=\frac{13}{5}$ [A1] expected gain $=\frac{13}{5}-3=-\frac{2}{5}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) a fair game has expected gain $0$, so the stake is $\$\frac{13}{5}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A game is fair when the expected prize equals the stake. Compute $E=\sum xP(x)$.

subtopic: Expected value and fair price of a game
statement: A raffle ticket wins nothing with probability $\frac58$, a $\$4$ prize with probability $\frac14$ and a $\$24$ prize with probability $\frac18$. (a) Find the expected gain of a player per game (the prize minus the stake of $\$6$). [3] (b) Find the stake that would make the game fair. [1]
markscheme: (a) expected prize $=\sum\text{prize}\times\text{probability}$ [M1] $=4$ [A1] expected gain $=4-6=-2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) a fair game has expected gain $0$, so the stake is $\$4$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A game is fair when the expected prize equals the stake. Compute $E=\sum xP(x)$.

subtopic: Family of power-law probability density functions on [0,1]
statement: This question investigates a family of continuous distributions. For a positive integer $n$, the random variable $X_n$ has probability density function $f(x)=(n+1)x^n$ for $0\le x\le1$, and $f(x)=0$ otherwise. (a) Show that $f$ is a valid probability density function. [2] (b) Show that $E(X_n)=\dfrac{n+1}{n+2}$. [3] (c) Find $E\left(X_n^2\right)$ and hence show that $\operatorname{Var}(X_n)=\dfrac{n+1}{(n+2)^2(n+3)}$. [4] (d) Show that the median of $X_n$ is $m_n=2^{-1/(n+1)}$, and find $m_1$, $m_2$ and $m_5$ to three significant figures. [4] (e) Let $Y=X_n^2$. By considering $P(Y\le y)$, show that $Y$ has probability density function $g(y)=\dfrac{n+1}{2}y^{(n-1)/2}$ for $0<y\le1$, and identify the distribution of $Y$ when $n=1$. [4] (f) Describe what happens to $E(X_n)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X_n)$ as $n\to\infty$, and interpret this. [3]
markscheme: (a) $f(x)\ge0$ on $[0,1]$ [R1] $\displaystyle\int_0^1(n+1)x^n\,dx=\left[x^{n+1}\right]_0^1=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $E(X_n)=\displaystyle\int_0^1x(n+1)x^n\,dx$ [M1] $=(n+1)\left[\dfrac{x^{n+2}}{n+2}\right]_0^1$ [A1] $=\dfrac{n+1}{n+2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $E(X_n^2)=\displaystyle\int_0^1(n+1)x^{n+2}\,dx=\dfrac{n+1}{n+3}$ [M1][A1] $\operatorname{Var}=\dfrac{n+1}{n+3}-\dfrac{(n+1)^2}{(n+2)^2}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{(n+1)\left[(n+2)^2-(n+1)(n+3)\right]}{(n+2)^2(n+3)}=\dfrac{n+1}{(n+2)^2(n+3)}$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $\displaystyle\int_0^m(n+1)x^n\,dx=m^{n+1}=\dfrac12$ [M1][A1] $m_n=2^{-1/(n+1)}$ so $m_1=0.707$, $m_2=0.794$, $m_5=0.891$ [A1] [A1] [4 marks] (e) $P(Y\le y)=P\left(X_n\le\sqrt y\right)$ [M1] $=\left(\sqrt y\right)^{n+1}=y^{(n+1)/2}$ [A1] differentiating: $g(y)=\dfrac{n+1}{2}y^{(n-1)/2}$ [A1] for $n=1$, $g(y)=1$ on $(0,1]$, so $Y$ is uniform on $[0,1]$ [A1] [4 marks] (f) $E(X_n)=\dfrac{n+1}{n+2}\to1$ [A1] $\operatorname{Var}(X_n)\to0$ since it behaves like $\dfrac1{n^2}$ [A1] the distribution concentrates near $x=1$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Parts (b) and (c) are straightforward integrals of powers of $x$. In (e) work from the cumulative distribution function and differentiate to get the pdf.

subtopic: Two-way table probabilities and independence
statement: A survey of 100 students recorded handedness and gender. The numbers of people in each category are: Left-handed and Male: 12; Left-handed and Female: 18; Right-handed and Male: 28; Right-handed and Female: 42. One person is chosen at random. Let $A$ be the event 'Left-handed' and $B$ the event 'Male'. (a) Find $P(A)$ and $P(A\cap B)$. [2] (b) Find $P(A\mid B)$. [2] (c) Determine whether $A$ and $B$ are independent, justifying your answer. [3]
markscheme: (a) $P(A)=\dfrac{30}{100}=\frac{3}{10}$ [A1] $P(A\cap B)=\dfrac{12}{100}=\frac{3}{25}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{12}{40}$ [M1] $=\frac{3}{10}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(B)=\dfrac{40}{100}=\frac{2}{5}$ [A1] $P(A)P(B)=\frac{3}{25}$ [M1] this equals $P(A\cap B)=\frac{3}{25}$, so $A$ and $B$ are independent [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Independence means $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$, equivalently $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$. Check it with exact fractions.

subtopic: Two-way table probabilities and independence
statement: A company surveyed 100 employees about how they travel to work. The numbers of people in each category are: Cycle and Under 30: 30; Cycle and 30 or over: 10; Drive and Under 30: 20; Drive and 30 or over: 40. One person is chosen at random. Let $A$ be the event 'Cycle' and $B$ the event 'Under 30'. (a) Find $P(A)$ and $P(A\cap B)$. [2] (b) Find $P(A\mid B)$. [2] (c) Determine whether $A$ and $B$ are independent, justifying your answer. [3]
markscheme: (a) $P(A)=\dfrac{40}{100}=\frac{2}{5}$ [A1] $P(A\cap B)=\dfrac{30}{100}=\frac{3}{10}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{30}{50}$ [M1] $=\frac{3}{5}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(B)=\dfrac{50}{100}=\frac{1}{2}$ [A1] $P(A)P(B)=\frac{1}{5}$ [M1] this is not equal to $P(A\cap B)=\frac{3}{10}$, so $A$ and $B$ are not independent [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Independence means $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$, equivalently $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$. Check it with exact fractions.

subtopic: Two-way table probabilities and independence
statement: A school surveyed 120 students about their diets. The numbers of people in each category are: Vegetarian and Year 12: 9; Vegetarian and Year 13: 21; Not vegetarian and Year 12: 27; Not vegetarian and Year 13: 63. One person is chosen at random. Let $A$ be the event 'Vegetarian' and $B$ the event 'Year 12'. (a) Find $P(A)$ and $P(A\cap B)$. [2] (b) Find $P(A\mid B)$. [2] (c) Determine whether $A$ and $B$ are independent, justifying your answer. [3]
markscheme: (a) $P(A)=\dfrac{30}{120}=\frac{1}{4}$ [A1] $P(A\cap B)=\dfrac{9}{120}=\frac{3}{40}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{9}{36}$ [M1] $=\frac{1}{4}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(B)=\dfrac{36}{120}=\frac{3}{10}$ [A1] $P(A)P(B)=\frac{3}{40}$ [M1] this equals $P(A\cap B)=\frac{3}{40}$, so $A$ and $B$ are independent [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Independence means $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$, equivalently $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$. Check it with exact fractions.

subtopic: Two-set Venn diagram counts
statement: A club surveys its members about two activities. Of $60$ people, $32$ play tennis, $28$ play chess, and $10$ do neither. (a) Find the number who do both. [3] (b) One person is chosen at random. Find the probability that the person does exactly one of the two activities. [2] (c) Given that the person chosen does at least one of the activities, find the probability that the person does both. [2]
markscheme: (a) $n(A\cup B)=60-10=50$ [A1] $n(A\cap B)=n(A)+n(B)-n(A\cup B)$ [M1] $=32+28-50=10$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) exactly one $=22+18=40$ [M1] probability $=\frac{2}{3}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{n(A\cap B)}{n(A\cup B)}=\dfrac{10}{50}$ [M1] $=\frac{1}{5}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use $n(A\cup B)=n(A)+n(B)-n(A\cap B)$, and fill in a Venn diagram starting from the intersection.

subtopic: Two-set Venn diagram counts
statement: A college surveyed its students. Of $80$ people, $45$ study French, $38$ study Spanish, and $12$ do neither. (a) Find the number who do both. [3] (b) One person is chosen at random. Find the probability that the person does exactly one of the two activities. [2] (c) Given that the person chosen does at least one of the activities, find the probability that the person does both. [2]
markscheme: (a) $n(A\cup B)=80-12=68$ [A1] $n(A\cap B)=n(A)+n(B)-n(A\cup B)$ [M1] $=45+38-68=15$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) exactly one $=30+23=53$ [M1] probability $=\frac{53}{80}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{n(A\cap B)}{n(A\cup B)}=\dfrac{15}{68}$ [M1] $=\frac{15}{68}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use $n(A\cup B)=n(A)+n(B)-n(A\cap B)$, and fill in a Venn diagram starting from the intersection.

subtopic: Union, intersection and independence
statement: The events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A)=0.4$, $P(B)=0.5$ and $P(A\cup B)=0.7$. (a) Find $P(A\cap B)$. [2] (b) Find $P(A\mid B)$. [2] (c) Hence state, with a reason, whether $A$ and $B$ are independent. [2] (d) Find $P(A'\cap B')$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$ [M1] $P(A\cap B)=0.4+0.5-0.7=0.2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{0.2}{0.5}$ [M1] $=0.4$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(A\mid B)=0.4=P(A)$ (or $P(A)P(B)=0.2=P(A\cap B)$) [M1] so $A$ and $B$ are independent [A1] [2 marks] (d) $1-P(A\cup B)=0.3$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Use the addition rule for the intersection. Independence holds exactly when $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.

subtopic: Mutually exclusive events versus independent events
statement: The events $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, with $P(A)=0.3$ and $P(B)=0.2$. (a) Find $P(A\cup B)$. [1] (b) Find $P(A'\cap B')$. [2] (c) Show that $A$ and $B$ are not independent. [3]
markscheme: (a) mutually exclusive so $P(A\cap B)=0$ and $P(A\cup B)=0.3+0.2=0.5$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $P(A'\cap B')=1-P(A\cup B)$ [M1] $=0.5$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) if independent, $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)=0.06$ [M1][A1] but $P(A\cap B)=0\ne0.06$, so they are not independent [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Mutually exclusive means $P(A\cap B)=0$. Two events with non-zero probabilities cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent.

subtopic: Total probability and conditional probability from a tree diagram
statement: For events $A$ and $B$, $P(A)=\dfrac38$, $P(B\mid A)=\dfrac23$ and $P(B\mid A')=\dfrac15$. (a) Find $P(A\cap B)$. [2] (b) Find $P(B)$. [3] (c) Find $P(A\mid B)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $P(A)\times P(B\mid A)=\dfrac38\times\dfrac23$ [M1] $=\frac{1}{4}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(A'\cap B)=\dfrac58\times\dfrac15=\frac{1}{8}$ [M1][A1] $P(B)=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{8}=\frac{3}{8}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}=\frac{1}{4}\div\frac{3}{8}$ [M1] $=\frac{2}{3}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Draw a tree: first split on $A$, then on $B$. Use the law of total probability for $P(B)$ and then divide for the conditional.

subtopic: Independence implies equal conditional probabilities
statement: The events $A$ and $B$ satisfy $P(A)=0.6$, $P(B\mid A)=0.5$ and $P(B\mid A')=0.5$. (a) Find $P(B)$. [2] (b) Hence show that $A$ and $B$ are independent. [2] (c) Hence write down $P(A'\cap B')$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $P(B)=0.6\times0.5+0.4\times0.5$ [M1] $=0.5$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(A\cap B)=0.6\times0.5=0.3$ [M1] $P(A)P(B)=0.6\times0.5=0.3$, so independent [R1] [2 marks] (c) $A'$ and $B'$ are also independent [M1] $P(A')P(B')=0.4\times0.5=0.2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: If $P(B\mid A)=P(B\mid A')$ then $B$ does not depend on $A$. Independence of $A$ and $B$ extends to their complements.

subtopic: Selection without replacement
statement: A bag contains $5$ red and $4$ blue counters. $3$ counters are drawn at random one after another without replacement. (a) Find the probability that all $3$ counters are red. [3] (b) Find the probability that exactly two of the $3$ counters are red. [3] (c) Given that the first counter drawn is blue, find the probability that the second is red. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{5}{9} \times \dfrac{4}{8} \times \dfrac{3}{7}$ [M1][A1] $=\frac{5}{42}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) number of ways: $\binom{5}{2}\binom{4}{1}=40$ out of $\binom{9}{3}=84$ [M1][A1] $=\frac{10}{21}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) after a blue is removed there are $8$ counters, $5$ red [M1] $=\frac{5}{8}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Without replacement the probabilities change after every draw. Multiply the successive conditional probabilities, or count favorable selections with combinations.

subtopic: Selection without replacement
statement: A bag contains $6$ red and $3$ blue counters. $3$ counters are drawn at random one after another without replacement. (a) Find the probability that all $3$ counters are red. [3] (b) Find the probability that exactly two of the $3$ counters are red. [3] (c) Given that the first counter drawn is blue, find the probability that the second is red. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{6}{9} \times \dfrac{5}{8} \times \dfrac{4}{7}$ [M1][A1] $=\frac{5}{21}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) number of ways: $\binom{6}{2}\binom{3}{1}=45$ out of $\binom{9}{3}=84$ [M1][A1] $=\frac{15}{28}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) after a blue is removed there are $8$ counters, $6$ red [M1] $=\frac{3}{4}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Without replacement the probabilities change after every draw. Multiply the successive conditional probabilities, or count favorable selections with combinations.

subtopic: Selection without replacement
statement: A bag contains $7$ red and $5$ blue counters. $4$ counters are drawn at random one after another without replacement. (a) Find the probability that all $4$ counters are red. [3] (b) Find the probability that exactly two of the $4$ counters are red. [3] (c) Given that the first counter drawn is blue, find the probability that the second is red. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{7}{12} \times \dfrac{6}{11} \times \dfrac{5}{10} \times \dfrac{4}{9}$ [M1][A1] $=\frac{7}{99}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) number of ways: $\binom{7}{2}\binom{5}{2}=210$ out of $\binom{12}{4}=495$ [M1][A1] $=\frac{14}{33}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) after a blue is removed there are $11$ counters, $7$ red [M1] $=\frac{7}{11}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Without replacement the probabilities change after every draw. Multiply the successive conditional probabilities, or count favorable selections with combinations.

subtopic: Bayes' theorem with several sources
statement: Three bakeries supply a store with loaves; a loaf is sub-standard with the stated probability. Bakery P produces $25\%$ of the items, Bakery Q $50\%$ and Bakery R $25\%$. The proportions of defective items are $10\%$, $5\%$ and $20\%$ respectively. (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen item is defective. [3] (b) Given that an item is defective, find the probability that it was produced by Bakery P. [3] (c) Which source is most likely to have produced a defective item? Give a reason. [1]
markscheme: (a) $P(D)=\sum P(\text{source})P(D\mid\text{source})$ [M1] $=\frac{1}{4}\times\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{2}\times\frac{1}{20}+\frac{1}{4}\times\frac{1}{5}$ [A1] $=\frac{1}{10}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $P(\text{Bakery P}\mid D)=\dfrac{\frac{1}{4}\times\frac{1}{10}}{\frac{1}{10}}$ [M1][A1] $=\frac{1}{4}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Bakery R, since it has the largest value of $P(\text{source})P(D\mid\text{source})$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Compute the joint probabilities for each source first; their sum is $P(D)$, and Bayes' theorem divides one joint probability by that sum.

subtopic: Probability using combinations
statement: A committee of $4$ people is chosen at random from $6$ men and $5$ women. (a) Find the probability that the committee contains exactly two women. [3] (b) Find the probability that the committee contains at least one woman. [2] (c) Find the probability that a particular man, Raj, is on the committee. [2]
markscheme: (a) total selections $\binom{11}{4}=330$ [A1] favorable $\binom52\binom62=150$ [M1] probability $=\frac{5}{11}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $1-P(\text{no women})=1-\dfrac{\binom64}{330}$ [M1] $=\frac{21}{22}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) favorable selections $\binom{10}{3}=120$ [M1] probability $=\dfrac{120}{330}=\frac{4}{11}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Count selections with combinations: favorable over total. For 'at least one', use the complement.

subtopic: Probability using combinations
statement: In a lottery, $6$ numbers are drawn at random without replacement from the integers $1$ to $30$. A player has chosen $6$ different numbers from the same set. (a) Find the probability that the player matches all six numbers. [2] (b) Find the probability that the player matches exactly two of the drawn numbers. [3] (c) Find the probability that the player matches at least three numbers. [3]
tips: Choose the matched numbers from the player's six and the unmatched from the other 24. Sum the relevant cases for 'at least'.

subtopic: Probability using combinations
statement: A hand of $5$ cards is dealt from a standard deck of $52$ cards, which has $13$ cards in each of $4$ suits. (a) Find the probability that the hand contains exactly two hearts. [3] (b) Find the probability that the hand contains no hearts. [2] (c) Find the probability that all five cards are of the same suit. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\binom{13}{2}\binom{39}{3}}{\binom{52}{5}}$ [M1][A1] $=0.274$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\binom{39}{5}}{\binom{52}{5}}$ [M1] $=0.222$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) for one suit $\binom{13}{5}$, for any suit $4\binom{13}{5}$ [M1][A1] probability $=\dfrac{4\binom{13}{5}}{\binom{52}{5}}=0.00198$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use combinations for unordered selections; condition on suits by choosing within each suit.

subtopic: Independent events leading to a quadratic equation
statement: The independent events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(B)=p$, $P(A)=2p$ and $P(A\cup B)=0.52$. (a) Show that $2p^2-3p+0.52=0$. [3] (b) Hence find $P(B)$, justifying your choice of root. [3]
tips: Independence gives $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. Reject any root that would make a probability exceed $1$.

subtopic: Independent events leading to a quadratic equation
statement: The independent events $A$ and $B$ satisfy $P(A)=p$, $P(B)=p+0.3$ and $P(A\cap B)=0.18$. (a) Show that $p^2+0.3p-0.18=0$. [2] (b) Find $P(A)$, justifying your choice of root. [3] (c) Find $P(A\cup B)$. [2]
tips: Form the equation from $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$ and discard any root outside $[0,1]$.

subtopic: Infinite geometric series in a game
statement: Anna and Ben take turns to roll a fair six-sided die, with Anna rolling first. The first person to roll a six wins the game. (a) Find the probability that Anna wins on her first roll, and the probability that Ben wins on his first roll. [2] (b) Show that the probability that Anna wins the game is $\dfrac{6}{11}$. [4] (c) Hence find the probability that Ben wins, and state who has the advantage. [2]
markscheme: (a) Anna: $\dfrac16$ [A1] Ben needs Anna to fail first: $\dfrac56\times\dfrac16=\dfrac5{36}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Anna wins on roll $1,3,5,\dots$: $\dfrac16+\left(\dfrac56\right)^2\dfrac16+\left(\dfrac56\right)^4\dfrac16+\dots$ [M1] geometric with first term $\dfrac16$, ratio $\dfrac{25}{36}$ [A1] $S_\infty=\dfrac{1/6}{1-25/36}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{1/6}{11/36}=\dfrac6{11}$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $1-\dfrac6{11}=\dfrac5{11}$ [A1] Anna has the advantage because she rolls first [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The probability of winning is a sum over the turns on which the player could win; each extra round multiplies by the probability that both players fail, giving an infinite geometric series.

subtopic: Infinite geometric series in a game
statement: Two players, Cara and Dev, alternately toss a fair coin, with Cara tossing first. The first player to toss a head wins. (a) Show that the probability that Cara wins on her $k$th toss is $\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac14\right)^{k-1}$. [3] (b) Hence find the probability that Cara wins. [3]
markscheme: (a) before Cara's $k$th toss there have been $k-1$ tosses by Cara and $k-1$ by Dev all tails [M1] probability $\left(\dfrac12\right)^{2(k-1)}\times\dfrac12$ [A1] $=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac14\right)^{k-1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\dfrac12\left(\dfrac14\right)^{k-1}$ is geometric with $a=\dfrac12$, $r=\dfrac14$ [M1] $S_\infty=\dfrac{1/2}{1-1/4}$ [M1] $=\dfrac23$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write the probability of a win at each possible turn, recognize the geometric series, and use $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ with $|r|<1$.

subtopic: Sample space for two dice
statement: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. Let $S$ be the sum of the scores, $M$ the event that at least one die shows $6$, and $N$ the event $S\ge9$. (a) Find $P(M)$. [2] (b) Find $P(N)$. [2] (c) Find $P(N\mid M)$. [3]
tips: List the sample space systematically (a $6\times6$ grid) and count outcomes: conditional probability restricts the sample space to the given event.

subtopic: Sample space for three dice
statement: Three fair four-sided dice, each numbered $1$ to $4$, are rolled. Let $S$ be the sum of the three scores and $P$ their product. (a) Find $P(S=9)$. [3] (b) Find the probability that $P$ is even. [2] (c) Given that $S=9$, find the probability that $P$ is even. [3]
markscheme: (a) total outcomes $4^3=64$ [A1] number of outcomes with sum $9$ is $10$ [M1] $P(S=9)=\frac{5}{32}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $P$ is odd only if all scores are odd: $\left(\dfrac12\right)^3=\dfrac18$ [M1] $P(P\text{ even})=\dfrac78$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) outcomes with $S=9$ and $P$ odd: $1$ [M1][A1] $P=\dfrac{9}{10}=\frac{9}{10}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: With three dice it is quicker to count outcomes with a systematic list than to draw a grid. A product is odd only when every factor is odd.

subtopic: Complementary probability: at least one
statement: A box contains $20$ components, of which $3$ are defective. Four components are chosen at random without replacement. (a) Find the probability that none of the chosen components is defective. [2] (b) Hence find the probability that at least one chosen component is defective. [1] (c) Find the probability that exactly one is defective. [2]
tips: 'At least one' is easiest by the complement. Use combinations since the selection is without replacement.

subtopic: Complementary probability: smallest number of trials
statement: A fair six-sided die is rolled $n$ times. (a) Find the probability of at least one six in four rolls. [2] (b) Find the smallest value of $n$ such that the probability of at least one six exceeds $0.9$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $1-\left(\dfrac56\right)^4$ [M1] $=0.518$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $1-\left(\dfrac56\right)^n>0.9$ [M1] $\left(\dfrac56\right)^n<0.1$ [A1] $n>\dfrac{\ln0.1}{\ln(5/6)}=12.63$ [M1] $n=13$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Use the complement: $P(\text{at least one six})=1-(5/6)^n$. Dividing by $\ln(5/6)<0$ reverses the inequality.

subtopic: Birthday problem
statement: Assume that each person's birthday is equally likely to be any of $365$ days, independently of others. (a) Find the probability that no two of $5$ people share a birthday. [2] (b) Hence find the probability that at least two of $5$ people share a birthday. [1] (c) Find the smallest group size $m$ for which this probability exceeds $0.5$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{365}{365}\times\dfrac{364}{365}\times\dfrac{363}{365}\times\dfrac{362}{365}\times\dfrac{361}{365}$ [M1] $=0.9729$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $1-0.9729=0.0271$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $P(m)=1-\dfrac{365\times364\times\cdots\times(365-m+1)}{365^m}$ [M1] evaluate for successive $m$ using a table or solver [M1] $m=22$ gives $0.476$ [A1] $m=23$ gives $0.507$ so $m=23$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Count the ways each new person can avoid all the previous birthdays. Use the table feature on your calculator to find where the probability first passes $0.5$.

subtopic: Conditional probability with a binomial distribution
statement: A student guesses the answer to each of $10$ multiple-choice questions, each with four options of which one is correct. Let $X$ be the number of correct answers. (a) Find $P(X\ge3)$. [2] (b) Given that the student gets at least $3$ correct, find the probability that exactly $4$ are correct. [3]
tips: $\{X=4\}$ is contained in $\{X\ge3\}$, so the intersection is just $P(X=4)$.

subtopic: Fibonacci numbers from consecutive heads in coin tosses
statement: This question investigates the probability that a fair coin tossed $n$ times never shows two heads in a row. Let $a_n$ be the number of sequences of $n$ tosses (each H or T) that contain no two consecutive heads. (a) List all the sequences for $n=3$, and hence write down $a_1$, $a_2$ and $a_3$. [3] (b) By considering the last toss, show that $a_n=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}$ for $n\ge3$. [4] (c) Hence find $a_8$ and the probability that $8$ tosses contain no two consecutive heads. [3] (d) Let $r=\lim_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{a_n}{a_{n-1}}$, assumed to exist. By dividing the recurrence by $a_{n-1}$, show that $r^2-r-1=0$ and find the exact value of $r$. [4] (e) Let $p_n=\dfrac{a_n}{2^n}$. Find the least $n$ for which $p_n<0.01$, and explain why $p_n$ decreases geometrically in the long run. [3]
markscheme: (a) for $n=3$: TTT, TTH, THT, HTT, HTH [A1] $a_1=2$ (H, T) and $a_2=3$ (TT, TH, HT) [A1] $a_3=5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) if the last toss is T, the first $n-1$ tosses can be any valid sequence: $a_{n-1}$ ways [M1][A1] if the last toss is H, the previous toss must be T, and the first $n-2$ tosses can be any valid sequence: $a_{n-2}$ ways [M1][A1] [4 marks] (c) $a_4=8,\ a_5=13,\ a_6=21,\ a_7=34$ [M1] $a_8=55$ [A1] probability $=\dfrac{55}{2^8}=\dfrac{55}{256}=0.215$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\dfrac{a_n}{a_{n-1}}=1+\dfrac{a_{n-2}}{a_{n-1}}$ [M1] in the limit $r=1+\dfrac1r$ [A1] $r^2-r-1=0$ [A1] $r=\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$ since $r>0$ [A1] [4 marks] (e) $p_n$ computed from $a_n$ (using the recurrence) [M1] $p_{22}=0.0111$ and $p_{23}=0.00894$ so $n=23$ [A1] $\dfrac{p_n}{p_{n-1}}\to\dfrac r2=0.809\dots<1$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Condition on the last toss to build the recurrence. For the limit, divide by the previous term and use the fact that the ratio converges. $a_n$ is a shifted Fibonacci sequence.

subtopic: Gambler's ruin: probability of reaching a target
statement: This question investigates the probability that a gambler reaches a target fortune. A gambler starts with $\$k$ and plays repeated games. In each game the gambler wins $\$1$ with probability $p=\dfrac35$ and loses $\$1$ with probability $q=\dfrac25$. Play stops when the gambler has $\$0$ (ruin) or $\$4$ (success). Let $h_k$ be the probability of reaching $\$4$ starting with $\$k$, so $h_0=0$ and $h_4=1$. (a) By considering the first game, show that $h_k=p\,h_{k+1}+q\,h_{k-1}$ for $k=1,2,3$, and write down the three equations for $h_1,h_2,h_3$. [3] (b) Show that $h_k=\dfrac{1-r^k}{1-r^4}$, where $r=\dfrac qp$, satisfies the recurrence in (a) and the conditions $h_0=0$, $h_4=1$. [4] (c) Evaluate $h_1$, $h_2$ and $h_3$ using $r=\dfrac23$. [3] (d) Verify that your values satisfy the three equations in (a). [2] (e) If the game is fair ($p=q=\dfrac12$), the recurrence becomes $h_k=\dfrac12(h_{k+1}+h_{k-1})$. Show that $h_k$ is an arithmetic sequence and find $h_1$, $h_2$ and $h_3$. [3]
markscheme: (a) after the first game the gambler has $\$(k+1)$ with probability $p$ or $\$(k-1)$ with probability $q$ [M1] law of total probability gives the relation [A1] $h_1=\dfrac35h_2$, $h_2=\dfrac35h_3+\dfrac25h_1$, $h_3=\dfrac35+\dfrac25h_2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) substitute $h_k=A+Br^k$: $p r^{k+1}+q r^{k-1}=r^{k-1}(pr^2+q)$ must equal $r^k$, so $pr^2-r+q=0$ [M1] factorise $(pr-q)(r-1)=0$ giving $r=\dfrac qp$ or $1$ [A1] $h_0=0$ gives $A+B=0$ [A1] $h_4=1$ gives $A+Br^4=1$, so $B=-\dfrac1{1-r^4}$, $A=\dfrac1{1-r^4}$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $1-r^4=\dfrac{65}{81}$ [M1] $h_1=\dfrac{1/3}{65/81}=\dfrac{27}{65}$ [A1] $h_2=\dfrac{9}{13}$ and $h_3=\dfrac{57}{65}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\dfrac35\times\dfrac9{13}=\dfrac{27}{65}=h_1$ [A1] $\dfrac35\times\dfrac{57}{65}+\dfrac25\times\dfrac{27}{65}=\dfrac{171+54}{325}=\dfrac{45}{65}=\dfrac9{13}$, and $\dfrac35+\dfrac25\times\dfrac9{13}=\dfrac{39+18}{65}=\dfrac{57}{65}$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) $h_{k+1}-h_k=h_k-h_{k-1}$, so the differences are constant [M1] $h_k=\dfrac k4$ using $h_0=0$ and $h_4=1$ [A1] $h_1=\dfrac14$, $h_2=\dfrac12$, $h_3=\dfrac34$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Condition on the first game to form the recurrence, then test the proposed closed form by substitution. For the fair case the middle term is the mean of its neighbors, which forces an arithmetic sequence.

subtopic: Linear regression, correlation and prediction from data
statement: Seven students recorded the hours they revised for a test and their scores. The following pairs (hours of revision $x$, test score $y$) were recorded: (2, 41); (3, 45); (5, 52); (6, 60); (8, 68); (9, 71); (11, 80). (a) Find the Pearson correlation coefficient $r$ and describe the strength and direction of the correlation. [3] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (c) Use your equation to estimate $y$ when $x=7$, and comment on the reliability of the estimate. [3]
markscheme: (a) $r=0.997$ [A1] positive correlation [A1] strong [A1] [3 marks] (b) gradient $4.396$ and intercept $31.94$ [M1] $y=4.396x+31.94$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y=4.396\times7+31.94=62.7$ [M1][A1] 7 lies inside the data range so the estimate is an interpolation and reasonably reliable [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Enter the data in two lists and use the calculator's linear regression. Predicting inside the range of the data (interpolation) is more reliable than predicting outside it (extrapolation).

subtopic: Linear regression, correlation and prediction from data
statement: The average outside temperature and the heating cost of a house were recorded for seven weeks. The following pairs (temperature $x$ (degrees C), heating cost $y$ (dollars)) were recorded: (5, 64); (8, 57); (12, 52); (15, 45); (18, 41); (22, 32); (25, 28). (a) Find the Pearson correlation coefficient $r$ and describe the strength and direction of the correlation. [3] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (c) Use your equation to estimate $y$ when $x=20$, and comment on the reliability of the estimate. [3]
markscheme: (a) $r=-0.998$ [A1] negative correlation [A1] strong [A1] [3 marks] (b) gradient $-1.797$ and intercept $72.53$ [M1] $y=-1.797x+72.53$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y=-1.797\times20+72.53=36.6$ [M1][A1] 20 lies inside the data range so the estimate is an interpolation and reasonably reliable [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Enter the data in two lists and use the calculator's linear regression. Predicting inside the range of the data (interpolation) is more reliable than predicting outside it (extrapolation).

subtopic: Linear regression, correlation and prediction from data
statement: A company recorded its advertising spend and sales over eight months. The following pairs (advertising spend $x$ (thousands of dollars), sales $y$ (thousands of units)) were recorded: (1, 3.1); (2, 4.8); (3, 5.2); (4, 7.9); (5, 8.1); (6, 10.4); (7, 10.9); (8, 13.2). (a) Find the Pearson correlation coefficient $r$ and describe the strength and direction of the correlation. [3] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (c) Use your equation to estimate $y$ when $x=12$, and comment on the reliability of the estimate. [3]
markscheme: (a) $r=0.989$ [A1] positive correlation [A1] strong [A1] [3 marks] (b) gradient $1.393$ and intercept $1.682$ [M1] $y=1.393x+1.682$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y=1.393\times12+1.682=18.4$ [M1][A1] 12 lies outside the data range so the estimate is an extrapolation and may be unreliable [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Enter the data in two lists and use the calculator's linear regression. Predicting inside the range of the data (interpolation) is more reliable than predicting outside it (extrapolation).

subtopic: Regression line from summary statistics
statement: Test scores in two subjects are compared. For $n$ pairs of data, $\bar x=20$, $\bar y=50$, the standard deviations are $s_x=4$ and $s_y=10$ and the correlation coefficient is $r=4/5$. (a) Find the gradient of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (c) Estimate $y$ when $x=24$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $b=r\dfrac{s_y}{s_x}=4/5\times\dfrac{10}{4}$ [M1] $=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) the line passes through $(\bar x,\bar y)$: $y-50=2(x-20)$ [M1] $y=2x+10$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y=58$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The regression line of $y$ on $x$ has gradient $r\,s_y/s_x$ and passes through the mean point $(\bar x,\bar y)$.

subtopic: Regression line from summary statistics
statement: The speed of a vehicle and its stopping distance are measured. For $n$ pairs of data, $\bar x=12$, $\bar y=30$, the standard deviations are $s_x=3$ and $s_y=6$ and the correlation coefficient is $r=-1/2$. (a) Find the gradient of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (c) Estimate $y$ when $x=10$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $b=r\dfrac{s_y}{s_x}=-1/2\times\dfrac{6}{3}$ [M1] $=-1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) the line passes through $(\bar x,\bar y)$: $y-30=-1(x-12)$ [M1] $y=-1x+42$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y=32$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The regression line of $y$ on $x$ has gradient $r\,s_y/s_x$ and passes through the mean point $(\bar x,\bar y)$.

subtopic: Finding the mean point and r from two regression lines
statement: The regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $y=\frac{3}{4}x+2$ and the regression line of $x$ on $y$ is $x=\frac{1}{3}y+1$. (a) Find the mean point $(\bar x,\bar y)$. [3] (b) Use the gradients to find the correlation coefficient $r$. [3]
markscheme: (a) both lines pass through the mean point [R1] solve simultaneously [M1] $\bar x=\frac{20}{9}$, $\bar y=\frac{11}{3}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $r^2=\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)=\frac{1}{4}$ [M1][A1] $r=\frac{1}{2}$, taking the sign of the gradient [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Both regression lines pass through $(\bar x,\bar y)$. The product of the two gradients is $r^2$, and $r$ has the same sign as the gradients.

subtopic: Finding the mean point and r from two regression lines
statement: The regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $y=-\frac{1}{2}x+10$ and the regression line of $x$ on $y$ is $x=-\frac{1}{2}y+14$. (a) Find the mean point $(\bar x,\bar y)$. [3] (b) Use the gradients to find the correlation coefficient $r$. [3]
markscheme: (a) both lines pass through the mean point [R1] solve simultaneously [M1] $\bar x=12$, $\bar y=4$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $r^2=\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{4}$ [M1][A1] $r=-\frac{1}{2}$, taking the sign of the gradient [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Both regression lines pass through $(\bar x,\bar y)$. The product of the two gradients is $r^2$, and $r$ has the same sign as the gradients.

subtopic: Fitting an exponential model y = ab^x using logarithms
statement: The number of bacteria $y$ (in thousands) in a culture at the end of $x$ hours is recorded: $(1,6.1),\ (2,9.2),\ (3,13.4),\ (4,20.5),\ (5,31.0),\ (6,45.2)$. A model of the form $y=ab^x$ is proposed. (a) Show that the model implies that $\ln y$ is linear in $x$. [2] (b) Find the regression line of $\ln y$ on $x$ and hence the values of $a$ and $b$. [4] (c) Estimate the number of bacteria after $8$ hours. [2] (d) State one reason why this estimate may be unreliable. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\ln y=\ln a+x\ln b$ [M1] which is linear in $x$ with gradient $\ln b$ and intercept $\ln a$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\ln y=0.4024x+1.406$ [M1][A1] $b=e^{0.4024}=1.50$ [A1] $a=e^{1.406}=4.08$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $y=4.08\times1.50^8$ [M1] $\approx102$ thousand [A1] [2 marks] (d) $x=8$ is outside the range of the data (extrapolation), and growth cannot continue unchecked [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Take natural logarithms of $y$, then run a linear regression of $\ln y$ against $x$. The intercept is $\ln a$ and the gradient is $\ln b$.

subtopic: Fitting a power model y = ax^b using logarithms
statement: The power $P$ (in watts) of a wind turbine at wind speed $v$ (meters per second) is recorded: $(1,3.1),\ (2,8.4),\ (4,24.5),\ (6,45.1),\ (8,70.3),\ (10,96.0)$. The model $P=av^b$ is proposed. (a) Show that $\ln P$ is a linear function of $\ln v$. [2] (b) Find the regression line of $\ln P$ on $\ln v$, and hence $a$ and $b$. [4] (c) Estimate the power when $v=5$ meters per second. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\ln P=\ln a+b\ln v$ [M1] linear in $\ln v$ with gradient $b$ and intercept $\ln a$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\ln P=1.502\ln v+1.115$ [M1][A1] $b=1.50$ [A1] $a=e^{1.115}=3.05$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $P=3.05\times5^{1.50}$ [M1] $=34.2$ watts [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Take logs of both variables. For a power model the gradient of the $\ln P$ against $\ln v$ line is the exponent $b$.

subtopic: Effect of an outlier on the correlation coefficient and regression line
statement: The pairs $(x,y)$: $(1,10),\ (2,12),\ (3,13),\ (4,15),\ (5,17),\ (6,18),\ (7,20),\ (8,22)$ are recorded. A ninth pair $(9,5)$ is later found to be a genuine measurement. (a) Find $r$ and the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$ for the original eight pairs. [3] (b) Find $r$ and the regression line for all nine pairs. [3] (c) Compare the two results and explain the effect of the ninth pair. [2]
markscheme: (a) $r=0.998$ [A1] $y=1.679x+8.321$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $r=0.233$ [A1] $y=0.4500x+12.42$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (c) the correlation is much weaker and the gradient much smaller [A1] the pair is far from the trend (an outlier) and has a large influence because it lies at the end of the $x$ range [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A single point far from the trend, especially one at the extreme of the $x$-range, can change both $r$ and the gradient markedly.

subtopic: Coded data and the regression line
statement: The number of subscribers $y$ (thousands) of a service in the years $2015$ to $2021$ is $120,\ 134,\ 149,\ 155,\ 171,\ 180,\ 196$. Let $t$ be the number of years after $2015$. (a) Find the regression line of $y$ on $t$. [2] (b) Interpret the gradient and the intercept in context. [2] (c) Use the model to estimate the number of subscribers in 2024 and comment on its reliability. [3]
markscheme: (a) data $(0,120),(1,134),\dots,(6,196)$ [M1] $y=12.21t+121.2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) each year the number of subscribers rises by about $12.2$ thousand [A1] at $t=0$ (the year 2015) the model gives about $121$ thousand subscribers [A1] [2 marks] (c) $t=9$: $y=12.21\times9+121.2=231.1$ [M1][A1] this is extrapolation beyond the data, so it may be unreliable [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Coding the year as $t=x-2015$ keeps the numbers small; the gradient is unchanged and only the intercept is affected.

subtopic: Arithmetic sequence from two terms
statement: The $p$th term of an arithmetic sequence is $u_p$. Given that $u_{3}=11$ and $u_{8}=31$: (a) Find the common difference $d$ and the first term $u_1$. [3] (b) Find the sum of the first $20$ terms. [2] (c) Which term of the sequence equals $91$? [2]
tips: Subtract two terms to find $d$, then use $u_n=u_1+(n-1)d$ and $S_n=\frac n2\left(2u_1+(n-1)d\right)$.

subtopic: Arithmetic sequence from two terms
statement: The $p$th term of an arithmetic sequence is $u_p$. Given that $u_{5}=-2$ and $u_{12}=26$: (a) Find the common difference $d$ and the first term $u_1$. [3] (b) Find the sum of the first $12$ terms. [2] (c) Which term of the sequence equals $106$? [2]
tips: Subtract two terms to find $d$, then use $u_n=u_1+(n-1)d$ and $S_n=\frac n2\left(2u_1+(n-1)d\right)$.

subtopic: Arithmetic sequence from two terms
statement: The $p$th term of an arithmetic sequence is $u_p$. Given that $u_{4}=17$ and $u_{9}=-8$: (a) Find the common difference $d$ and the first term $u_1$. [3] (b) Find the sum of the first $15$ terms. [2] (c) Which term of the sequence equals $-98$? [2]
tips: Subtract two terms to find $d$, then use $u_n=u_1+(n-1)d$ and $S_n=\frac n2\left(2u_1+(n-1)d\right)$.

subtopic: Geometric sequence from two terms
statement: The terms of a geometric sequence are all positive, with $u_{2}=12$ and $u_{5}=96$. (a) Find the common ratio $r$ and the first term $u_1$. [3] (b) Find the sum of the first $8$ terms. [2] (c) Explain why the sequence has no sum to infinity. [1]
markscheme: (a) $r^{3}=\dfrac{96}{12}$ [M1] $r=2$ [A1] $u_1=\dfrac{12}{2^{1}}=6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $S_{8}=\dfrac{6\left(1-2^{8}\right)}{1-2}$ [M1] $=1530$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $r=2>1$, so the terms grow and the series diverges [R1] [1 mark]
tips: From two terms of a geometric sequence, divide to get $r^{k}$ where $k$ is the gap in positions. Use $S_\infty=\dfrac{u_1}{1-r}$ only when $|r|<1$.

subtopic: Geometric sequence from two terms
statement: The terms of a geometric sequence are all positive, with $u_{2}=12$ and $u_{4}=3$. (a) Find the common ratio $r$ and the first term $u_1$. [3] (b) Find the sum of the first $6$ terms. [2] (c) Find the sum to infinity. [2]
tips: From two terms of a geometric sequence, divide to get $r^{k}$ where $k$ is the gap in positions. Use $S_\infty=\dfrac{u_1}{1-r}$ only when $|r|<1$.

subtopic: Geometric sequence from two terms
statement: The terms of a geometric sequence are all positive, with $u_{3}=27$ and $u_{6}=1$. (a) Find the common ratio $r$ and the first term $u_1$. [3] (b) Find the sum of the first $5$ terms. [2] (c) Find the sum to infinity. [2]
tips: From two terms of a geometric sequence, divide to get $r^{k}$ where $k$ is the gap in positions. Use $S_\infty=\dfrac{u_1}{1-r}$ only when $|r|<1$.

subtopic: Convergence of a geometric series with a parameter
statement: A geometric series has first term $4$ and common ratio $\dfrac{x}{3}$, where $x$ is a real number. (a) Find the set of values of $x$ for which the series converges. [2] (b) Given that the sum to infinity is $6$, find $x$. [3] (c) Find the sum to infinity when $x=-2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\left|\dfrac x3\right|<1$ [M1] $-3<x<3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{4}{1-\frac x3}=6$ [M1] $1-\dfrac x3=\dfrac23$ [A1] $x=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $r=-\dfrac23$ [A1] $S_\infty=\dfrac{4}{1+\frac23}=\dfrac{12}{5}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A geometric series converges exactly when $|r|<1$. Then $S_\infty=\dfrac{u_1}{1-r}$.

subtopic: Convergence of a geometric series with a parameter
statement: Consider the infinite geometric series $1+(2x-1)+(2x-1)^2+\dots$ (a) Find the values of $x$ for which the series converges. [3] (b) Find, in terms of $x$, the sum to infinity, simplifying your answer. [2] (c) Given that the sum to infinity is $\dfrac52$, find $x$. [2]
tips: Write down the common ratio first, then impose $|r|<1$. Check that your final $x$ lies in the interval of convergence.

subtopic: Compound interest with regular deposits
statement: At the start of each year a person deposits $\$1200$ into an account paying $4.5\%$ interest per year, compounded annually. The first deposit is made at the start of year 1. (a) Show that the value of the account at the end of year 3, immediately after interest is added, is $1200\left(1.045^3+1.045^2+1.045\right)$. [2] (b) Find the value of the account at the end of year $10$. [3] (c) Find the number of years needed for the account to first exceed $\$24000$. [3]
markscheme: (a) first deposit grows for 3 years: $1200\times1.045^3$ [M1] second for 2 years and third for 1 year, so total $=1200\left(1.045^3+1.045^2+1.045\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) geometric series with first term $1200\times1.045$ and ratio $1.045$ [M1] $S_{10}=\dfrac{1200\times1.045\left(1.045^{10}-1\right)}{1.045-1}$ [M1] $=\$15409.41$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) solve $\dfrac{1200\times1.045\left(1.045^n-1\right)}{0.045}>24000$ with a table or solver [M1][A1] $n=15$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Each deposit earns interest for a different number of years, so the amounts form a geometric series. Use $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$ with $a=\text{deposit}\times(1+i)$.

subtopic: Compound interest with regular deposits
statement: At the start of each year a person deposits $\$500$ into an account paying $3\%$ interest per year, compounded annually. The first deposit is made at the start of year 1. (a) Show that the value of the account at the end of year 3, immediately after interest is added, is $500\left(1.03^3+1.03^2+1.03\right)$. [2] (b) Find the value of the account at the end of year $15$. [3] (c) Find the number of years needed for the account to first exceed $\$10000$. [3]
markscheme: (a) first deposit grows for 3 years: $500\times1.03^3$ [M1] second for 2 years and third for 1 year, so total $=500\left(1.03^3+1.03^2+1.03\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) geometric series with first term $500\times1.03$ and ratio $1.03$ [M1] $S_{15}=\dfrac{500\times1.03\left(1.03^{15}-1\right)}{1.03-1}$ [M1] $=\$9578.44$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) solve $\dfrac{500\times1.03\left(1.03^n-1\right)}{0.03}>10000$ with a table or solver [M1][A1] $n=16$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Each deposit earns interest for a different number of years, so the amounts form a geometric series. Use $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$ with $a=\text{deposit}\times(1+i)$.

subtopic: Evaluating a sum in sigma notation
statement: Consider $S=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{20}3 k + 1$. (a) Write down the first three terms of the sum and state the type of series, if it is arithmetic or geometric. [3] (b) Evaluate $S$. [2]
markscheme: (a) first terms $4,\ 7,\ 10$ [A1] common difference $3$ [A1] arithmetic [A1] [3 marks] (b) use the sum formula or the calculator's sum function [M1] $S=650.0$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For an arithmetic series use $S_n=\frac n2(u_1+u_n)$ with $u_1=4$ and $u_{20}=61$.

subtopic: Evaluating a sum in sigma notation
statement: Consider $S=\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{10}5 \left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^{k}$. (a) Write down the first three terms of the sum and state the type of series, if it is arithmetic or geometric. [3] (b) Evaluate $S$. [2]
markscheme: (a) first terms $5,\ 4,\ 3.2$ [A1] common ratio $0.8$ [A1] geometric [A1] [3 marks] (b) use the sum formula or the calculator's sum function [M1] $S=22.85$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A geometric series has $S_n=u_1\dfrac{1-r^n}{1-r}$, here with $11$ terms starting at $k=0$.

subtopic: Evaluating a sum in sigma notation
statement: Consider $S=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{15}k^{2} + 2 k$. (a) Write down the first three terms of the sum and state the type of series, if it is arithmetic or geometric. [3] (b) Evaluate $S$. [2]
markscheme: (a) first terms $3,\ 8,\ 15$ [A1] differences $5,7$ are not constant and ratios are not constant [A1] neither arithmetic nor geometric [A1] [3 marks] (b) use the sum formula or the calculator's sum function [M1] $S=1480$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: When a sum is neither arithmetic nor geometric, enter the general term into the calculator's summation function.

subtopic: Smallest n for a sum to exceed a value
statement: An arithmetic sequence has first term $7$ and common difference $5$. (a) Write an expression for $S_n$, the sum of the first $n$ terms. [2] (b) Find the smallest value of $n$ for which $S_n>1000$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $S_n=\dfrac n2\left(2\times7+(n-1)\times5\right)$ [M1] $=\dfrac n2\left(5n+9\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac n2\left(5n+9\right)>1000$ [M1] solve using a table or the quadratic [A1] $S_{19}=988.000$ and $S_{20}=1090.00$, so $n=20$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Form the quadratic inequality in $n$, or use a table of values of $S_n$ and look for the first value above the target.

subtopic: Smallest n for a sum to exceed a value
statement: An arithmetic sequence has first term $4$ and common difference $3$. (a) Write an expression for $S_n$, the sum of the first $n$ terms. [2] (b) Find the smallest value of $n$ for which $S_n>800$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $S_n=\dfrac n2\left(2\times4+(n-1)\times3\right)$ [M1] $=\dfrac n2\left(3n+5\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac n2\left(3n+5\right)>800$ [M1] solve using a table or the quadratic [A1] $S_{22}=781.000$ and $S_{23}=851.000$, so $n=23$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Form the quadratic inequality in $n$, or use a table of values of $S_n$ and look for the first value above the target.

subtopic: Smallest n for a geometric sum to exceed a value
statement: A geometric sequence has first term $3$ and common ratio $1.2$. (a) Write down an expression for $S_n$. [1] (b) Find the smallest $n$ such that $S_n>200$. [4]
