markscheme: (a) $f(-x)=-x^3+x=-f(x)$ [M1][A1] rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin [A1] [3 marks] (b) $g(a+h)=f(h)$ and $g(a-h)=f(-h)=-f(h)$ [M1][A1] so $g(a+h)+g(a-h)=0$: point symmetry about $(a,0)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) centre of symmetry of $f$ is $(0,0)$, moved to $(a,c)$ [M1] $a=2$, $c=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $f'(x)=3x^2-1$ so $x=\pm\dfrac1{\sqrt3}$ [M1] $f\left(-\dfrac1{\sqrt3}\right)=\dfrac2{3\sqrt3}$ and $f\left(\dfrac1{\sqrt3}\right)=-\dfrac2{3\sqrt3}$ [A1] new maximum $\left(2-\dfrac1{\sqrt3},3+\dfrac2{3\sqrt3}\right)$ [A1] new minimum $\left(2+\dfrac1{\sqrt3},3-\dfrac2{3\sqrt3}\right)$, the midpoint of the two points is $(2,3)$ [A1] [4 marks] (e) $|f(-x)|=|f(x)|$ when $f$ is odd or even [M1] for $f(x)=x^3-x$, $|f(-x)|=|-f(x)|=|f(x)|$ [A1] so the graph of $|f|$ is symmetric about the $y$-axis [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A translation moves the centre of symmetry with it. Symmetry statements follow from $f(a+h)\pm f(a-h)$.

subtopic: The remainder theorem and the factor theorem
statement: The polynomial $p(x)=2x^3+ax^2-7x+b$ has a factor $(x-2)$ and leaves remainder $-12$ when divided by $(x+1)$. (a) Write down two equations in $a$ and $b$. [3] (b) Find $a$ and $b$. [3] (c) Hence factorize $p(x)$ completely. [3]
tips: If $(x-k)$ is a factor then $p(k)=0$; the remainder on division by $(x-k)$ is $p(k)$.

subtopic: Sum and product of the roots of a cubic
statement: The roots of $2x^3-3x^2+4x-5=0$ are $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$. (a) Write down $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$, $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma$. [3] (b) Find the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$ and hence explain why the equation cannot have three real roots. [3] (c) Find the value of $\dfrac1\alpha+\dfrac1\beta+\dfrac1\gamma$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\dfrac32$ [A1] $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=2$ [A1] $\alpha\beta\gamma=\dfrac52$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2\left(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha\right)$ [M1] $=\dfrac94-4=-\dfrac74$ [A1] a sum of squares of real numbers cannot be negative, so not all roots are real [R1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha}{\alpha\beta\gamma}$ [M1] $=\dfrac45$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For $ax^3+bx^2+cx+d=0$: sum of roots $-b/a$, sum of pairwise products $c/a$, product $-d/a$.

subtopic: Roots in arithmetic progression
statement: The roots of $x^3-12x^2+kx-28=0$ are in arithmetic progression. (a) Write the roots as $a-d$, $a$ and $a+d$ and show that $a=4$. [2] (b) Use the product of the roots to find $d^2$, and hence find the roots. [3] (c) Find $k$. [2]
markscheme: (a) sum of roots $=3a=12$ [M1] $a=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $a\left(a^2-d^2\right)=28$ [M1] $4\left(16-d^2\right)=28$, $d^2=9$ [A1] roots $1,4,7$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $k=1\times4+4\times7+7\times1$ [M1] $=39$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Choosing the middle root $a$ as the centre simplifies the sum of the roots to $3a$.

subtopic: Polynomial division and factorization
statement: Let $p(x)=x^4-3x^3-7x^2+27x-18$. (a) Show that $x=2$ and $x=3$ are roots of $p(x)=0$. [2] (b) Hence factorize $p(x)$ completely. [3] (c) Solve $p(x)>0$. [3]
tips: After finding two roots, divide by the product of the corresponding linear factors, then factorize the quotient.

subtopic: Cubic inequality
markscheme: critical values $-2,1,4$ [A1] sign analysis: positive for $x>4$, negative on $(1,4)$, positive on $(-2,1)$, negative for $x<-2$ [M1][A1] $x\le-2$ or $1\le x\le4$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Mark the roots on a number line and test one value in each interval.

subtopic: Complex roots of a quartic with real coefficients
statement: The polynomial $p(x)=x^4-2x^3+3x^2-2x+2$ has real coefficients, and $x=1+\mathrm i$ is a root. (a) Write down another root of $p(x)=0$ and the quadratic factor of $p(x)$ with real coefficients that they generate. [3] (b) Find the other two roots. [4]
markscheme: (a) $1-\mathrm i$ [A1] $(x-1)^2+1=x^2-2x+2$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (b) divide: $x^4-2x^3+3x^2-2x+2=\left(x^2-2x+2\right)\left(x^2+1\right)$ [M1][A1] $x^2+1=0$ [M1] $x=\pm\mathrm i$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Complex roots come in conjugate pairs, so the product of their linear factors is a real quadratic.

subtopic: Roots of a quintic with a calculator
statement: Consider $p(x)=x^5-4x^4-3x^3+14x^2-8x+5$. (a) Use your calculator to find all the real roots of $p(x)=0$ to three significant figures. [2] (b) State the sum of all five roots (real and complex) and verify it using the roots found by the solver. [3]
markscheme: (a) polynomial solver or graph [M1] $x=3.98$, $x=-2.04$, $x=1.60$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) sum of roots $=4$ [A1] sum of the real parts of all five roots $=4.00$ [M1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: A polynomial solver returns complex roots as well; Vieta's formula gives an independent check of the sum.

subtopic: Power sums of the roots of a cubic
statement: The roots of $x^3-x^2-x-1=0$ are $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$. Let $s_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n+\gamma^n$. (a) Find $s_0$, $s_1$ and $s_2$. [4] (b) Show that $s_{n+3}=s_{n+2}+s_{n+1}+s_n$ for $n\ge0$. [3] (c) Hence find $s_3,\ s_4,\ s_5$ and $s_6$. [3] (d) The equation has one real root $\alpha\approx1.84$ and two complex roots with $|\beta|<1$. Explain why $\dfrac{s_{n+1}}{s_n}\to\alpha$ as $n\to\infty$. [3] (e) Compute $\dfrac{s_6}{s_5}$ and compare it with the real root found by your calculator. [2]
markscheme: (a) $s_0=3$ [A1] $s_1=1$ [A1] $s_2=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2\left(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha\right)$ [M1] $=1-2(-1)=3$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) each root satisfies $x^3=x^2+x+1$ [M1] multiply by $x^n$: $x^{n+3}=x^{n+2}+x^{n+1}+x^n$ [A1] sum over the three roots [A1] [3 marks] (c) $s_3=3+1+3=7$ [A1] $s_4=7+3+1=11$ [A1] $s_5=21$, $s_6=39$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $|\beta|=|\gamma|<1$ so $\beta^n,\gamma^n\to0$ [A1] $s_n\approx\alpha^n$ for large $n$ [M1] hence $\dfrac{s_{n+1}}{s_n}\to\alpha$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $\dfrac{39}{21}=1.857$ [A1] the real root is $1.839$, close [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Each root satisfies the cubic, so every power sum satisfies the same recurrence as the coefficients. The dominant real root controls the long-term growth.

subtopic: Modulus inequality solved algebraically
tips: $|u|<k$ means $-k<u<k$; $|u|\ge k$ means $u\ge k$ or $u\le-k$.

subtopic: Equation with two modulus terms
tips: Squaring removes the modulus signs since $|u|^2=u^2$; check by substituting back.

subtopic: Sum of two modulus functions
statement: Let $f(x)=|x|+|x-2|$. (a) Express $f(x)$ without modulus signs for $x<0$, $0\le x\le2$ and $x>2$. [3] (b) Hence solve $f(x)\le4$. [3] (c) State the minimum value of $f$ and the set of $x$ at which it occurs. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x<0$: $-2x+2$ [A1] $0\le x\le2$: $2$ [A1] $x>2$: $2x-2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $-2x+2\le4$ gives $x\ge-1$ [M1] $2x-2\le4$ gives $x\le3$ [A1] $-1\le x\le3$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) minimum $2$ [A1] for $0\le x\le2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Split at the points where each modulus expression changes sign. $|x|+|x-2|$ is the sum of the distances from $x$ to $0$ and to $2$.

subtopic: Rational inequality
statement: Solve $\dfrac{x+1}{x-2}\ge3$. [6]
markscheme: $\dfrac{x+1}{x-2}-3\ge0$ [M1] $\dfrac{x+1-3x+6}{x-2}=\dfrac{7-2x}{x-2}\ge0$ [A1] critical values $x=2$ and $x=\dfrac72$ [A1] sign test [M1] $2<x\le\dfrac72$ [A1] $x=2$ excluded since the denominator is zero [R1] [6 marks]
tips: Never multiply by an expression of unknown sign; bring everything to one side and analyze the sign of the combined fraction.

subtopic: Solving a modulus equation with a calculator
statement: Solve $|x^2-5x+2|=3x-4$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. [5]
markscheme: consider the two cases $x^2-5x+2=\pm(3x-4)$ [M1] $x^2-8x+6=0$ gives $x=4\pm\sqrt{10}$ [A1] $x^2-2x-2=0$ gives $x=1\pm\sqrt3$ [A1] require $3x-4\ge0$, i.e. $x\ge\dfrac43$ [R1] solutions $x=4+\sqrt{10}=7.16$ and $x=1+\sqrt3=2.73$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Each solution must satisfy $3x-4\ge0$, since a modulus cannot equal a negative number; check all candidate roots.

subtopic: Absolute value and distance: a graphical interpretation
statement: (a) Interpret $|x-4|<2$ as a statement about distance on the number line and solve it. [2] (b) Solve $|x-4|<2$ and $|x+1|>3$ simultaneously. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x$ is less than $2$ units from $4$ [R1] $2<x<6$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $|x+1|>3$ gives $x>2$ or $x<-4$ [M1][A1] intersect with $2<x<6$: $2<x<6$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Distances on the number line give a quick way to see the answer; check by sketching the intervals.

subtopic: Modulus function with a parameter
statement: Consider the equation $|x-2|=k-x$ where $k$ is a constant. (a) Solve the equation for $x\ge2$ and for $x<2$, in terms of $k$. [4] (b) Hence state the number of solutions when $k<2$, $k=2$ and $k>2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x\ge2$: $x-2=k-x$ so $x=\dfrac{k+2}2$ [A1] valid if $\dfrac{k+2}2\ge2$, i.e. $k\ge2$ [A1] $x<2$: $2-x=k-x$ so $k=2$ [A1] and every $x<2$ is a solution when $k=2$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $k<2$: none [A1] $k>2$: one solution $x=\dfrac{k+2}2$ [A1] $k=2$: infinitely many, all $x\le2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Solve each branch separately and check the branch condition. The left side is a V-shape, the right side a line of gradient $-1$.

subtopic: Rational inequality with a quadratic denominator
statement: Find the set of values of $x$ for which $\dfrac{x^2-4}{x^2-1}<0$. [6]
markscheme: numerator zeros $\pm2$, denominator zeros $\pm1$ [A1] sign chart on $(-\infty,-2),(-2,-1),(-1,1),(1,2),(2,\infty)$ [M1] positive, negative, positive, negative, positive [A1] negative on $(-2,-1)$ and $(1,2)$ [A1] $-2<x<-1$ or $1<x<2$ [A1] endpoints excluded: strict inequality and the denominator is undefined at $\pm1$ [R1] [6 marks]
tips: Factorize numerator and denominator, list all critical values, and use a sign chart.

subtopic: Maclaurin series from derivatives
statement: Let $f(x)=\ln(1+\sin x)$. (a) Find $f(0)$, $f'(x)$ and $f'(0)$. [3] (b) Find $f''(0)$. [3] (c) Hence write down the Maclaurin series of $f(x)$ up to and including the $x^2$ term. [2]
tips: The Maclaurin series of $f$ is $f(0)+f'(0)x+\dfrac{f''(0)}{2!}x^2+\dots$

subtopic: Product of Maclaurin series
statement: (a) Write down the Maclaurin series of $\mathrm e^{2x}$ up to the $x^3$ term and of $\cos x$ up to the $x^2$ term. [2] (b) Hence find the Maclaurin series of $\mathrm e^{2x}\cos x$ up to and including the $x^3$ term. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm e^{2x}=1+2x+2x^2+\dfrac43x^3+\dots$ [A1] $\cos x=1-\dfrac{x^2}2+\dots$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) multiply the series [M1] $x^0$: $1$ [A1] $x^2$: $2-\dfrac12=\dfrac32$ and $x^3$: $\dfrac43-1=\dfrac13$ [A1] $\mathrm e^{2x}\cos x\approx1+2x+\dfrac32x^2+\dfrac13x^3$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Multiply known series term by term and collect powers of $x$, keeping only terms up to the required order.

subtopic: Using Maclaurin series to evaluate a limit
statement: (a) Write down the Maclaurin series of $\sin x$ up to the $x^5$ term and of $\mathrm e^x$ up to the $x^3$ term. [2] (b) Hence find $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{\sin x-x}{x^3}$. [3] (c) Hence find $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{\mathrm e^x-1-x-\frac{x^2}2}{x^3}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\sin x=x-\dfrac{x^3}6+\dfrac{x^5}{120}$ [A1] $\mathrm e^x=1+x+\dfrac{x^2}2+\dfrac{x^3}6$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\left(x-\frac{x^3}6+\dots\right)-x}{x^3}$ [M1] $=-\dfrac16+\dfrac{x^2}{120}-\dots$ [A1] limit $=-\dfrac16$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{\frac{x^3}6+\dots}{x^3}$ [M1] $=\dfrac16$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Substitute the series and cancel the lowest powers; the limit is the ratio of the leading coefficients.

subtopic: Maclaurin series of a binomial-type function
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac1{\sqrt{1-2x}}$ for $|x|<\dfrac12$. (a) Use the binomial series to find the expansion of $f(x)$ up to the $x^3$ term. [4] (b) Hence find an approximation for $\dfrac1{\sqrt{0.8}}$ by substituting $x=0.1$, and compare with the calculator value. [2]
markscheme: (a) $(1-2x)^{-1/2}=1+\left(-\dfrac12\right)(-2x)+\dfrac{\left(-\frac12\right)\left(-\frac32\right)}{2}(-2x)^2+\dfrac{\left(-\frac12\right)\left(-\frac32\right)\left(-\frac52\right)}{6}(-2x)^3$ [M1][A1] $=1+x+\dfrac32x^2+\dfrac52x^3$ [A1][A1] [4 marks] (b) $1+0.1+0.015+0.0025=1.1175$ [A1] calculator $1.1180$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The Maclaurin series of $(1+u)^n$ is the binomial series with $u=-2x$.

subtopic: Estimating an integral using a Maclaurin series
statement: (a) Find the Maclaurin series of $\mathrm e^{-x^2}$ up to and including the $x^6$ term. [3] (b) Hence estimate $\displaystyle\int_0^{1}\mathrm e^{-x^2}\,dx$. [3] (c) Compare your answer with the value given by your calculator, and state the percentage error. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm e^u=1+u+\dfrac{u^2}2+\dfrac{u^3}6$ with $u=-x^2$ [M1] $1-x^2+\dfrac{x^4}2-\dfrac{x^6}6$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) integrate term by term [M1] $\left[x-\dfrac{x^3}3+\dfrac{x^5}{10}-\dfrac{x^7}{42}\right]_0^1$ [A1] $=0.74286$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) calculator: $0.746824$ [A1] percentage error $=0.53\%$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Substitute $-x^2$ into the series for $\mathrm e^u$ and integrate each term; the truncated series gives an approximation, not an exact value.

subtopic: Series for ln(1+x) and an approximation
statement: The Maclaurin series of $\ln(1+x)$ is $x-\dfrac{x^2}2+\dfrac{x^3}3-\dfrac{x^4}4+\dots$ for $-1<x\le1$. (a) Use the first four terms with $x=0.2$ to approximate $\ln1.2$. [3] (b) Find the absolute error compared with the calculator value $\ln1.2$. [2] (c) Explain why the series would be a poor approximation for $\ln3$ with $x=2$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $0.2-0.02+\dfrac{0.008}3-\dfrac{0.0016}4$ [M1][A1] $=0.18227$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\ln1.2=0.182322$ [A1] error $=0.000055$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $x=2$ lies outside the interval of convergence $-1<x\le1$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: A Maclaurin approximation is accurate near $x=0$ and only converges inside its radius of convergence.

subtopic: Maclaurin series of arctan and an approximation of pi
statement: (a) Given that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\arctan x=\dfrac1{1+x^2}$, use the expansion of $\dfrac1{1+x^2}$ to show that $\arctan x=x-\dfrac{x^3}3+\dfrac{x^5}5-\dots$. [4] (b) Use $\arctan1=\dfrac\pi4$ and the first four terms to approximate $\pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac1{1+x^2}=1-x^2+x^4-\dots$ [M1][A1] integrate term by term [M1] $\arctan x=x-\dfrac{x^3}3+\dfrac{x^5}5-\dots$ since $\arctan0=0$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\dfrac\pi4\approx1-\dfrac13+\dfrac15-\dfrac17$ [M1] $=0.7238$ [A1] $\pi\approx2.895$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Integrate the geometric series $1-x^2+x^4-\dots$ term by term; the constant of integration is $0$ because $\arctan0=0$.

subtopic: Series solution of a differential equation
statement: This question uses Maclaurin series to solve $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y+x$ with $y(0)=1$. (a) Find $y'(0)$, then differentiate the equation to find $y''(0)$, $y'''(0)$ and $y^{(4)}(0)$. [4] (b) Hence write down the Maclaurin series for $y$ up to and including the $x^4$ term. [3] (c) Verify that $y=2\mathrm e^x-x-1$ satisfies the differential equation and the initial condition. [3] (d) Expand $2\mathrm e^x-x-1$ as a Maclaurin series up to $x^4$ and compare with part (b). [3] (e) Use the series with $x=0.5$ to estimate $y(0.5)$ and compare with the exact value. [2]
tips: Differentiate the equation repeatedly and evaluate at $x=0$ using the initial condition. The result matches the expansion of the exact solution.

subtopic: Using a series to find a higher derivative at zero
statement: Let $f(x)=\mathrm e^x\sin x$. (a) Find the Maclaurin series of $f(x)$ up to and including the $x^4$ term by multiplying the standard series. [4] (b) Hence write down $f'(0)$, $f''(0)$ and $f'''(0)$. [3] (c) Verify $f''(0)$ by differentiating $f$ directly. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\left(1+x+\dfrac{x^2}2+\dfrac{x^3}6\right)\left(x-\dfrac{x^3}6\right)$ [M1][A1] $x^3$ coefficient: $\dfrac12-\dfrac16=\dfrac13$ [A1] $f(x)=x+x^2+\dfrac{x^3}3+0\,x^4+\dots$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) coefficient of $x^n$ is $\dfrac{f^{(n)}(0)}{n!}$ [M1] $f'(0)=1$, $f''(0)=2$ [A1] $f'''(0)=3!\times\dfrac13=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $f'(x)=\mathrm e^x(\sin x+\cos x)$, $f''(x)=2\mathrm e^x\cos x$ [M1] $f''(0)=2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The coefficient of $x^n$ in the Maclaurin series is $f^{(n)}(0)/n!$, so derivatives at $0$ can be read from a series.

subtopic: Solving a system of three linear equations
statement: Consider the system $\begin{cases} x+y+z=6 \\ 2x-y+z=3 \\ x+2y-z=2 \end{cases}$ (a) Solve the system by elimination. [4] (b) State the determinant of the coefficient matrix and explain what it tells you about the solution. [2]
markscheme: (a) eliminate one variable from two pairs of equations [M1] obtain a $2\times2$ system [A1] $x=1$ [A1] $y=2$ and $z=3$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\det=7\ne0$ [A1] so there is a unique solution (the three planes meet at a single point) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Eliminate the same variable from two different pairs of equations to reduce to two equations in two unknowns.

subtopic: Solving a system of three linear equations
statement: Consider the system $\begin{cases} 2x+y-z=1 \\ x-2y+3z=9 \\ 3x+y+2z=13 \end{cases}$ (a) Solve the system by elimination. [4] (b) State the determinant of the coefficient matrix and explain what it tells you about the solution. [2]
markscheme: (a) eliminate one variable from two pairs of equations [M1] obtain a $2\times2$ system [A1] $x=\frac{3}{2}$ [A1] $y=\frac{3}{2}$ and $z=\frac{7}{2}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\det=-14\ne0$ [A1] so there is a unique solution (the three planes meet at a single point) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A non-zero determinant guarantees a unique solution.

subtopic: Solving a system of three linear equations
statement: A shop sells three products with prices $x$, $y$, $z$ dollars. Consider the system $\begin{cases} 3x+2y+z=11 \\ x-y+2z=7 \\ 2x+3y-2z=1 \end{cases}$ (a) Solve the system using your calculator. [3] (b) State the determinant of the coefficient matrix and explain what it tells you about the solution. [2]
markscheme: (a) enter the augmented matrix or use the system solver [M1] $x=2.000$ [A1] $y=1.000$, $z=3.000$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\det=5\ne0$ [A1] so there is a unique solution (the three planes meet at a single point) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the system solver and check the solution in one of the equations.

subtopic: Solving a system of three linear equations
statement: Consider the system $\begin{cases} x+2y+3z=14 \\ 2x-y+z=3 \\ 4x+y-2z=0 \end{cases}$ (a) Solve the system using your calculator. [3] (b) State the determinant of the coefficient matrix and explain what it tells you about the solution. [2]
markscheme: (a) enter the augmented matrix or use the system solver [M1] $x=1.000$ [A1] $y=2.000$, $z=3.000$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\det=35\ne0$ [A1] so there is a unique solution (the three planes meet at a single point) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the simultaneous equation solver on your calculator.

subtopic: Conditions for no solution or infinitely many solutions
statement: Consider the system $\begin{cases} x+2y-z=1 \\ 2x+5y-3z=3 \\ x+3y+kz=m \end{cases}$ where $k$ and $m$ are constants. (a) Show that eliminating $x$ from the first two equations gives $y-z=1$. [2] (b) Eliminate $x$ from the first and third equations, and hence find the value of $k$ for which the system does not have a unique solution. [4] (c) For $k=-2$, find the value of $m$ for which the system has infinitely many solutions, and the value of $m$ for which it has no solution. [3] (d) Describe the geometrical arrangement of the three planes when $k=-2$ and $m=2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $(2x+5y-3z)-2(x+2y-z)=3-2$ [M1] $y-z=1$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $(x+3y+kz)-(x+2y-z)=m-1$ gives $y+(k+1)z=m-1$ [M1][A1] subtract $y-z=1$: $(k+2)z=m-2$ [M1] no unique solution when $k+2=0$, $k=-2$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $0\cdot z=m-2$ [M1] infinitely many solutions when $m=2$ [A1] no solution when $m\ne2$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) the planes share a common line [A1] forming a sheaf (they meet along a line) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Reduce to a single equation in $z$; a zero coefficient on the left with a non-zero right side means inconsistency.

subtopic: A system with a linear and a quadratic equation
statement: Solve the system $y=2x-1$ and $x^2+y^2=13$. [6]
tips: Substitute the linear equation into the quadratic one and solve; do not forget the corresponding $y$-values.

subtopic: Three planes with a linear dependence
statement: Three planes have equations $x+y+z=3$, $x-y+2z=2$ and $2x+3z=k$, where $k$ is a constant. (a) Show that the three planes have no common point unless $k$ takes one particular value, and find that value. [3] (b) For this value of $k$, find a vector equation of the line of intersection of the three planes. [3]
markscheme: (a) adding the first two equations gives $2x+3z=5$ [M1][A1] this contradicts the third equation unless $k=5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) let $z=t$: $x=\dfrac{5-3t}2$ [M1] $y=3-x-t=\dfrac{1+t}2$ [A1] $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 5/2 \\ 1/2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} -3/2 \\ 1/2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Look for a linear dependence between the equations: if the third is a combination of the first two, the planes share a line when consistent and have no common point otherwise.

subtopic: Fitting a quadratic through three points
statement: A parabola $y=ax^2+bx+c$ passes through the points $(1,2)$, $(2,5)$ and $(3,12)$. (a) Write down three equations for $a$, $b$ and $c$. [2] (b) Solve the system using your calculator, and write down the equation of the parabola. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the vertex. [2]
tips: Substitute each point to form a linear system in $a$, $b$, $c$.

subtopic: A word problem leading to a linear system
statement: A theater sells adult, child and senior tickets. On one day $120$ tickets were sold for a total of $\$1080$. Adult tickets cost $\$12$, child tickets $\$7$ and senior tickets $\$9$. The number of adult tickets sold was twice the number of senior tickets. (a) Let $a$, $c$ and $s$ be the numbers of adult, child and senior tickets. Write down three equations. [3] (b) Solve the system. [3]
tips: Define variables, translate each sentence into an equation, then eliminate.

subtopic: Classifying the solutions of a system with a parameter
statement:
This question investigates the system $x+y+z=1$, $x+2y+3z=4$, $x+4y+az=b$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants. (a) Eliminate $x$ to obtain two equations in $y$ and $z$. [3] (b) Show that the system has a unique solution if and only if $a
e7$. [3] (c) For $a
e7$, find $x$, $y$, $z$ in terms of $a$ and $b$. [4] (d) Describe the solution set when $a=7$ for $b=10$ and for $b
e10$. [3] (e) Find the solution when $a=3$ and $b=2$ and check it in all three equations. [2]
markscheme:
(a) second minus first: $y+2z=3$ [M1][A1] third minus first: $3y+(a-1)z=b-1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) substitute $y=3-2z$: $9-6z+(a-1)z=b-1$ [M1] $(a-7)z=b-10$ [A1] a unique $z$ exists iff $a
e7$ [R1] [3 marks] (c) $z=\dfrac{b-10}{a-7}$ [A1] $y=3-2z=\dfrac{3a-21-2b+20}{a-7}=\dfrac{3a-2b-1}{a-7}$ [A1] $x=1-y-z=\dfrac{a-7-3a+2b+1-b+10}{a-7}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{-2a+b+4}{a-7}$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $b=10$: $0z=0$, infinitely many solutions on a line [A1] $b
e10$: $0=b-10
e0$, no solutions [A1] geometrically: three planes meeting in a line, or forming a triangular prism [A1] [3 marks] (e) $z=\dfrac{-8}{-4}=2$, $y=\dfrac{9-4-1}{-4}=-1$, $x=\dfrac{-6+2+4}{-4}=0$ [A1] check: $0-1+2=1$, $0-2+6=4$, $0-4+6=2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Eliminate one variable at a time; the coefficient $(a-7)$ of $z$ in the reduced equation decides between unique, none or infinitely many solutions.

subtopic: Asymptotes and intercepts of a rational function
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{3x-6}{x^2-x-6}$ for $x\in\mathbb R$, $x\ne3$, $x\ne-2$. (a) Find the equations of all asymptotes. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the axis intercepts. [2] (c) Determine whether the graph crosses its horizontal asymptote. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x^2-x-6=(x-3)(x+2)$ so vertical asymptotes $x=3$ and $x=-2$ [A1][A1] horizontal asymptote $y=0$ (degree of numerator is smaller) [A1] [3 marks] (b) $y$-intercept: $f(0)=\dfrac{-6}{-6}=1$, $(0,1)$ [A1] $x$-intercept: $3x-6=0$, $(2,0)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $f(x)=0$ at $x=2$ [M1] so it crosses $y=0$ at $(2,0)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Vertical asymptotes come from the zeros of the denominator not cancelled by the numerator. A horizontal asymptote can be crossed at finite $x$.

subtopic: Oblique asymptote and range
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2-3x+4}{x-1}$ for $x\ne1$. (a) Show that $f(x)=x-2+\dfrac2{x-1}$ and write down the equations of the asymptotes. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the local maximum and local minimum. [4] (c) Hence state the range of $f$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x^2-3x+4=(x-1)(x-2)+2$ [M1][A1] asymptotes $x=1$ and $y=x-2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f'(x)=1-\dfrac2{(x-1)^2}=0$ [M1] $(x-1)^2=2$, $x=1\pm\sqrt2$ [A1] $f(1-\sqrt2)=-1-2\sqrt2$ is a local maximum [A1] $f(1+\sqrt2)=-1+2\sqrt2$ is a local minimum [A1] [4 marks] (c) $y\le-1-2\sqrt2$ or $y\ge-1+2\sqrt2$ [A1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: Polynomial division gives the oblique asymptote. The range of a function with a gap comes from the local extrema.

subtopic: Partial fractions and integration of a rational function
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{5x+7}{(x+1)(x+2)}$. (a) Express $f(x)$ in the form $\dfrac A{x+1}+\dfrac B{x+2}$. [3] (b) Find $\displaystyle\int_0^2f(x)\,dx$, giving the answer in the form $\ln\left(\dfrac pq\right)$. [4]
tips: Use partial fractions to split the integrand into two logarithmic terms and combine the logarithms at the end.

subtopic: Rational inequality using a graph and algebra
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{2x}{x+1}$ and $g(x)=x$. (a) Solve $f(x)=g(x)$. [3] (b) Hence solve $f(x)>g(x)$. [4]
tips: Bring the inequality to one side with a common denominator and use a sign chart; the denominator's zero gives a break in the intervals.

subtopic: A rational function with a parameter and the discriminant
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}\ (x\in\mathbb R)$. By considering the equation $f(x)=k$, find the range of $f$. [6]
markscheme: $\dfrac x{x^2+1}=k$ gives $kx^2-x+k=0$ [M1][A1] for real $x$ with $k\ne0$ need $\Delta=1-4k^2\ge0$ [M1] $-\dfrac12\le k\le\dfrac12$ [A1] $k=0$ is attained at $x=0$ [A1] range $\left[-\dfrac12,\dfrac12\right]$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: A value $k$ is in the range exactly when $f(x)=k$ has a real solution; the discriminant of the resulting quadratic gives the allowed $k$.

subtopic: The graph of a rational function with a calculator
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2-4}{x^2+x+1}$. (a) Find the zeros of $f$ and the equation of its horizontal asymptote. [3] (b) Use your calculator to find the coordinates of the local minimum and local maximum. [3] (c) Find the point where the graph crosses its horizontal asymptote. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x^2-4=0$ so $x=\pm2$ [A1][A1] $y=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) graph $f$ and use the minimum and maximum functions [M1] local minimum $(-0.417,-5.06)$ [A1] local maximum $(-9.58,1.06)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $f(x)=1$: $x^2-4=x^2+x+1$ [M1] $x=-5$, so $(-5,1)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Graph $f$ and use the calculator's minimum and maximum functions; the denominator is always positive so there are no vertical asymptotes.

subtopic: Drug concentration modeled by a rational function
statement: The concentration $C$ mg/L of a drug in the blood $t$ hours after an injection is modeled by $C(t)=\dfrac{20t}{t^2+4}$ for $t\ge0$. (a) Find the concentration after $1$ hour. [1] (b) Find the time at which the concentration is greatest and the maximum concentration. [4] (c) Find the times at which the concentration is $4$ mg/L. [3] (d) State what happens to the concentration in the long term. [1]
tips: Differentiate with the quotient rule and set the numerator to zero. The horizontal asymptote $y=0$ describes the long-term behavior.

subtopic: Fixed points of a rational function
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x+6}{x+2}$ for $x\ne-2$. (a) Find the values of $x$ for which $f(x)=x$. [3] (b) Find $f(f(x))$ and show that its fixed points are the same as those of $f$. [4]
tips: A fixed point satisfies $f(x)=x$. Fixed points of $f$ are also fixed points of $f\circ f$.

subtopic: Sketching 1/f from a rational function
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x-1}{x+2}$ and $g(x)=\dfrac1{f(x)}$. (a) Write down the asymptotes of $f$ and of $g$. [4] (b) Find the axis intercepts of $f$ and of $g$. [3] (c) Solve $f(x)=g(x)$. [3]
tips: The vertical asymptotes of $1/f$ are at the zeros of $f$, and the zeros of $1/f$ are at the vertical asymptotes of $f$.

subtopic: A family of rational functions f(x) = x/(x^2+a)
statement: This question investigates the family $f_a(x)=\dfrac{x}{x^2+a}$ where $a>0$. (a) Show that $f_a$ is an odd function and state the horizontal asymptote. [3] (b) Show that $f_a'(x)=\dfrac{a-x^2}{\left(x^2+a\right)^2}$ and find the coordinates of the stationary points in terms of $a$. [4] (c) Hence state the range of $f_a$ in terms of $a$. [2] (d) Show that the second derivative is $f_a''(x)=\dfrac{2x\left(x^2-3a\right)}{\left(x^2+a\right)^3}$ and find the $x$-coordinates of the points of inflection. [4] (e) Show that the stationary points of $f_a$ for different values of $a$ all lie on the curve $y=\dfrac1{2x}$ and that the points of inflection with $x=\sqrt{3a}$ all lie on a curve to be found. [3]
markscheme: (a) $f_a(-x)=\dfrac{-x}{x^2+a}=-f_a(x)$ [M1][A1] $y=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) quotient rule: $\dfrac{\left(x^2+a\right)-x(2x)}{\left(x^2+a\right)^2}$ [M1][A1] zero when $x=\pm\sqrt a$ [A1] points $\left(\sqrt a,\dfrac1{2\sqrt a}\right)$ and $\left(-\sqrt a,-\dfrac1{2\sqrt a}\right)$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) maximum value $\dfrac1{2\sqrt a}$ and minimum $-\dfrac1{2\sqrt a}$ [M1] range $\left[-\dfrac1{2\sqrt a},\dfrac1{2\sqrt a}\right]$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) differentiate the quotient [M1][A1] the numerator vanishes at $x=0$ and $x=\pm\sqrt{3a}$ [A1] $f''$ changes sign at each, so three points of inflection [A1] [4 marks] (e) for $x=\sqrt a$: $y=\dfrac1{2\sqrt a}=\dfrac1{2x}$ [A1] for $x=\sqrt{3a}$: $y=\dfrac{\sqrt{3a}}{4a}=\dfrac{3}{4x}$ [M1] curve $y=\dfrac3{4x}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the quotient rule twice and factorize. Eliminating the parameter $a$ between the coordinates of the special points gives a locus.

subtopic: Separable differential equation with an initial condition
statement: Given that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac xy$ and $y=3$ when $x=4$, with $y>0$: (a) Find $y$ in terms of $x$. [5] (b) State the domain of the solution. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\int y\,dy=\int x\,dx$ [M1] $\dfrac{y^2}2=\dfrac{x^2}2+c$ [A1] $9=16+k$ so $k=-7$ in $y^2=x^2+k$ [M1][A1] $y=\sqrt{x^2-7}$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $x>\sqrt7$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Separate the variables, integrate both sides, then use the initial condition to find the constant.

subtopic: Separable differential equation with a trigonometric factor
statement: A function $y(x)$ satisfies $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y\cos x$ with $y(0)=2$. (a) Find $y$ in terms of $x$. [4] (b) Find the maximum value of $y$ and the least positive value of $x$ at which it occurs. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\int\dfrac{dy}y=\int\cos x\,dx$ [M1] $\ln y=\sin x+c$ [A1] $y=A\mathrm e^{\sin x}$ [A1] $y(0)=2$ gives $A=2$, $y=2\mathrm e^{\sin x}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) maximum when $\sin x=1$ [M1] $y=2\mathrm e$ at $x=\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Separate to $\dfrac1y\,dy=\cos x\,dx$ and integrate; exponentiate and absorb the constant into $A$.

subtopic: Homogeneous differential equation using y = vx
statement: Consider $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{x+y}x$ for $x>0$, with $y=0$ when $x=1$. (a) Use the substitution $y=vx$ to show that $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=1$. [3] (b) Hence solve the differential equation. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}$ [M1] $v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=1+v$ [A1] $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=1$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) $\int dv=\int\dfrac1x\,dx$ [M1] $v=\ln x+c$ [A1] $y=x\ln x+cx$ [A1] $y(1)=0$ gives $c=0$, $y=x\ln x$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: For a homogeneous equation substitute $y=vx$, use the product rule for $dy/dx$, and separate $v$ and $x$.

subtopic: First-order linear equation using an integrating factor
statement: Solve $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+2y=\mathrm e^{-x}$ given that $y=3$ when $x=0$. [6]
markscheme: integrating factor $\mathrm e^{\int2\,dx}=\mathrm e^{2x}$ [M1][A1] $\dfrac d{dx}\left(y\mathrm e^{2x}\right)=\mathrm e^{x}$ [M1] $y\mathrm e^{2x}=\mathrm e^x+c$ [A1] $y=\mathrm e^{-x}+c\mathrm e^{-2x}$ and $3=1+c$ [M1] $y=\mathrm e^{-x}+2\mathrm e^{-2x}$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: Multiply by $\mathrm e^{\int P\,dx}$ so the left side becomes a single derivative.

subtopic: Integrating factor with a variable coefficient
statement: Solve $x\dfrac{dy}{dx}-2y=x^3$ for $x>0$, given that $y=0$ when $x=1$. [6]
markscheme: divide by $x$: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}-\dfrac2xy=x^2$ [M1] integrating factor $\mathrm e^{-2\ln x}=x^{-2}$ [M1][A1] $\dfrac d{dx}\left(\dfrac y{x^2}\right)=1$ [A1] $\dfrac y{x^2}=x+c$ with $c=-1$ [A1] $y=x^3-x^2$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: Put the equation in the standard form $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)$ before finding the integrating factor.

subtopic: Euler's method for dy/dx = x + y
statement: Consider $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x+y$ with $y=1$ when $x=0$. Euler's method with step size $h=0.1$ is used. (a) Use Euler's method $y_{n+1}=y_n+hf(x_n,y_n)$ to find $y_1$ and $y_2$. [3] (b) Continue to estimate $y$ at $x=0.5$. [2] (c) The exact solution is $y=2\mathrm e^x-x-1$. Find the percentage error in your estimate at $x=0.5$. [3]
tips: Each Euler step moves along the tangent: $y_{n+1}=y_n+h\,f(x_n,y_n)$. Smaller steps reduce the error.

subtopic: Euler's method for a non-separable equation
statement: A function satisfies $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x^2+y^2$ with $y(0)=1$. (a) Use Euler's method with $h=0.1$ to estimate $y(0.2)$. [4] (b) Explain why the actual value of $y(0.2)$ is likely to be larger than your estimate. [1]
markscheme: (a) $y_1=1+0.1(0+1)=1.100$ [A1] $y_2=y_1+0.1\left(0.1^2+y_1^2\right)$ [M1] $=1.1+0.1(0.01+1.21)$ [A1] $=1.222$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $y''$ is positive ($y$ is convex), so the tangent line lies below the curve and Euler's method underestimates [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Euler's method follows tangent lines; for a convex solution the tangent lines are below the curve.

subtopic: Newton's law of cooling
statement: A cup of coffee at $90^\circ$C is placed in a room at $20^\circ$C. Its temperature $T$ satisfies $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-20)$, where $t$ is in minutes. After $10$ minutes its temperature is $50^\circ$C. (a) Show that $T=20+70\mathrm e^{-kt}$. [4] (b) Find the value of $k$. [2] (c) Find the time for the coffee to cool to $30^\circ$C. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\int\dfrac{dT}{T-20}=-\int k\,dt$ [M1] $\ln(T-20)=-kt+c$ [A1] $T-20=A\mathrm e^{-kt}$ [A1] $T(0)=90$ gives $A=70$ [A1] [AG] [4 marks] (b) $30=70\mathrm e^{-10k}$ [M1] $k=0.0847$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $10=70\mathrm e^{-kt}$ [M1] $t=23.0$ minutes [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The rate is proportional to the difference from room temperature, so separate $T-20$ from $t$.

subtopic: Population with constant harvesting
statement: A fish population $P$ satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.1P-50$, where $t$ is in years, with $P(0)=400$. (a) Find the equilibrium population and explain why it is unstable. [2] (b) Solve the differential equation to show that $P=500-100\mathrm e^{0.1t}$. [4] (c) Find the time at which the population dies out. [2]
markscheme: (a) $0.1P-50=0$ gives $P=500$ [A1] below $500$ the rate is negative and above it is positive, so the population moves away from $500$ [R1] [2 marks] (b) $\int\dfrac{dP}{0.1P-50}=\int dt$ [M1] $10\ln|0.1P-50|=t+c$ [A1] $0.1P-50=A\mathrm e^{0.1t}$ with $A=-10$ [A1] $P=500-100\mathrm e^{0.1t}$ [A1] [AG] [4 marks] (c) $500=100\mathrm e^{0.1t}$ [M1] $t=10\ln5=16.1$ years [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Separate the variables and integrate with a logarithm. Constant harvesting makes the equilibrium unstable.

subtopic: The logistic differential equation
statement: This question investigates the logistic model $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.2P\left(1-\dfrac P{1000}\right)$ for a population $P$ with $P(0)=100$. (a) Find the values of $P$ for which the population is in equilibrium. [1] (b) Show that $\dfrac{1}{P\left(1-\frac P{1000}\right)}=\dfrac1P+\dfrac1{1000-P}$. [2] (c) Hence solve the differential equation to show that $P=\dfrac{1000}{1+9\mathrm e^{-0.2t}}$. [6] (d) Find the time at which the population first reaches $500$. [2] (e) Show that the rate of growth $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$ is greatest when $P=500$ and find this greatest rate. [3] (f) State the limit of $P$ as $t\to\infty$ and interpret it. [1]
markscheme: (a) $P=0$ and $P=1000$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\dfrac{1000}{P(1000-P)}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{(1000-P)+P}{P(1000-P)}=\dfrac1P+\dfrac1{1000-P}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\int\left(\dfrac1P+\dfrac1{1000-P}\right)dP=\int0.2\,dt$ [M1] $\ln P-\ln(1000-P)=0.2t+c$ [A1] $\dfrac P{1000-P}=A\mathrm e^{0.2t}$ [A1] $P(0)=100$ gives $A=\dfrac19$ [A1] solve for $P$: $P=\dfrac{1000}{1+9\mathrm e^{-0.2t}}$ [M1][A1] [6 marks] (d) $1+9\mathrm e^{-0.2t}=2$ [M1] $t=5\ln9=10.99$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.2P-\dfrac{0.2P^2}{1000}$, a downward parabola in $P$ [M1] maximum at $P=500$ [A1] rate $=0.2\times500\times0.5=50$ [A1] [3 marks] (f) $P\to1000$, the carrying capacity of the environment [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Separate the variables and use partial fractions. The logistic curve is S-shaped with its steepest growth at half the carrying capacity.

subtopic: Cosine rule, sine rule and area of a triangle
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $BC=7.2$ cm, $AC=5.4$ cm and angle $ACB=68^\circ$. (a) Find $AB$. [3] (b) Find the size of angle $BAC$. [3] (c) Find the area of the triangle. [2]
tips: Use the cosine rule when two sides and the included angle are known. The area is $\frac12ab\sin C$.

subtopic: Triangle given three sides
statement: A triangle has sides of length $9$ cm, $7$ cm and $12$ cm. (a) Find the size of the largest angle. [3] (b) Find the area of the triangle. [3] (c) Find the radius of the inscribed circle, using area $=rs$ where $s$ is the semi-perimeter. [2]
markscheme: (a) the largest angle is opposite the side $12$ [R1] $\cos\theta=\dfrac{9^2+7^2-12^2}{2\times9\times7}$ [M1] $\theta=96.38^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac12(9)(7)\sin96.38^\circ$ [M1][A1] $=31.30\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $s=14$ [A1] $r=\dfrac{31.30}{14}=2.24$ cm [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Find the largest angle with the cosine rule (it is opposite the longest side). The inradius satisfies area $=rs$.

subtopic: Exact values in a triangle with a 30 degree angle
statement: In triangle $ABC$, angle $B=30^\circ$, $AB=6$ and $BC=4\sqrt3$. (a) Find $AC$ exactly. [3] (b) Use the sine rule to find angle $A$. [3] (c) Find the exact area of the triangle. [1]
markscheme: (a) $AC^2=6^2+\left(4\sqrt3\right)^2-2(6)\left(4\sqrt3\right)\cos30^\circ$ [M1] $=36+48-48\sqrt3\times\dfrac{\sqrt3}2=84-72$ [A1] $AC^2=12$ so $AC=2\sqrt3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\sin A}{4\sqrt3}=\dfrac{\sin30^\circ}{2\sqrt3}$ [M1] $\sin A=1$ [A1] $A=90^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac12(6)(2\sqrt3)=6\sqrt3$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Compute $\cos30^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}2$ exactly; a right angle appears when $\sin A=1$.

subtopic: Trigonometry in a square-based pyramid
statement: A pyramid $VABCD$ has a horizontal square base $ABCD$ of side $8$ cm. The vertex $V$ is vertically above the centre $M$ of the base, with $VM=10$ cm. (a) Find the length of $AC$ and of $AM$. [2] (b) Find the length of the slant edge $VA$ and the angle between $VA$ and the base. [4] (c) Find the angle between the face $VAB$ and the base. [3]
markscheme: (a) $AC=8\sqrt2=11.31$ cm [A1] $AM=5.657$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) $VA=\sqrt{10^2+32.00}=11.49$ cm [M1][A1] $\tan\theta=\dfrac{10}{5.657}$ [M1] $\theta=60.5^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) let $N$ be the midpoint of $AB$, $MN=4$ [A1] $\tan\phi=\dfrac{10}4$ [M1] $\phi=68.2^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Draw right triangles using the vertical height. The angle between a face and the base is measured along a line perpendicular to their common edge.

subtopic: The space diagonal of a cuboid
statement: A cuboid $ABCDEFGH$ has base $ABCD$ with $AB=6$ cm, $BC=4$ cm and height $AE=3$ cm. (a) Find the length of the diagonal $AG$. [3] (b) Find the angle between $AG$ and the base $ABCD$. [3] (c) Find the angle between $AG$ and the edge $AB$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $AC=\sqrt{36+16}$ [M1] $AG=\sqrt{36+16+9}$ [A1] $=7.810$ cm [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\tan\theta=\dfrac{CG}{AC}=\dfrac3{\sqrt{52}}$ [M1][A1] $\theta=22.6^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\cos\alpha=\dfrac{\overrightarrow{AG}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB}}{|AG||AB|}=\dfrac6{7.810}$ [M1][A1] $\alpha=39.8^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Find the base diagonal first, then use Pythagoras again. The angle with an edge uses the scalar product or a right triangle.

subtopic: Angles of elevation of a tower from two points
statement: From a point $A$ on level ground the angle of elevation of the top $T$ of a vertical tower is $25^\circ$. From a point $B$, $50$ m closer to the tower and in line with it and $A$, the angle of elevation is $40^\circ$. (a) Show that angle $ATB=15^\circ$. [2] (b) Use the sine rule in triangle $ATB$ to find $BT$. [3] (c) Find the height of the tower. [2]
markscheme: (a) exterior angle of triangle $ATB$ at $B$ is $40^\circ$ [M1] $\angle ATB=40^\circ-25^\circ=15^\circ$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{BT}{\sin25^\circ}=\dfrac{50}{\sin15^\circ}$ [M1][A1] $BT=81.64$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) $h=BT\sin40^\circ$ [M1] $=52.5$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the exterior angle theorem to find the angle at the top, then the sine rule to get a side, then a right triangle for the height.

subtopic: Bearings and the cosine rule
statement: A ship sails $12$ km on a bearing of $040^\circ$ from port $P$ to a point $Q$. It then sails $9$ km on a bearing of $170^\circ$ to a point $R$. (a) Show that angle $PQR=50^\circ$. [2] (b) Find the distance $PR$. [3] (c) Find the bearing of $R$ from $P$. [3]
markscheme: (a) the bearing of $P$ from $Q$ is $040^\circ+180^\circ=220^\circ$ [M1] angle $PQR=220^\circ-170^\circ=50^\circ$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $PR^2=12^2+9^2-2(12)(9)\cos50^\circ$ [M1][A1] $PR=9.282$ km [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{\sin\angle RPQ}{9}=\dfrac{\sin50^\circ}{9.282}$ [M1] $\angle RPQ=48.0^\circ$ [A1] bearing $=040^\circ+48.0^\circ=88.0^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Draw a diagram with north lines at each point. Co-interior and back-bearing angles give the angle in the triangle.

subtopic: Chords and tangents of a circle
statement: A circle has centre $O$ and radius $5$ cm. A chord $AB$ has length $8$ cm, and $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$. (a) Find $OM$. [2] (b) Find the size of angle $AOB$ in radians, to three significant figures. [3] (c) The tangents at $A$ and $B$ meet at $T$. Find $OT$ and the length $AT$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $OM\perp AB$ and $AM=4$ [M1] $OM=\sqrt{25-16}=3$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\sin\dfrac{\theta}2=\dfrac45$ [M1][A1] $\theta=2\arcsin0.8=1.85$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $OA\perp AT$ and $\cos\dfrac\theta2=\dfrac35$ so $OT=\dfrac{5}{3/5}=\dfrac{25}3$ [M1][A1] $AT=\sqrt{\dfrac{625}9-25}=\dfrac{20}3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The radius to a chord's midpoint is perpendicular to the chord; the radius to a point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent.

subtopic: A cyclic quadrilateral
statement: The quadrilateral $ABCD$ is cyclic with $AB=5$, $BC=7$, $CD=6$ and $DA=4$ (in cm). (a) Let $AC=x$. Use the cosine rule in triangles $ABC$ and $ADC$ and the fact that $\angle ABC+\angle ADC=180^\circ$ to show that $\dfrac{74-x^2}{70}=-\dfrac{52-x^2}{48}$. [4] (b) Solve for $x$, giving the answer to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the area of the quadrilateral. [3]
tips: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, so their cosines are negatives and their sines are equal.

subtopic: Triangle in the coordinate plane: midpoints, bisectors and area
statement: The vertices of a triangle are $A(1,2)$, $B(7,4)$ and $C(3,8)$. (a) Find the midpoint $M$ of $BC$ and the gradient of $AM$. [3] (b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. [3] (c) Find the area of the triangle. [2]
markscheme: (a) $M=\left(\dfrac{7+3}2,\dfrac{4+8}2\right)=(5,6)$ [A1] gradient $=\dfrac{6-2}{5-1}$ [M1] $=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) midpoint $(4,3)$ [A1] gradient of $AB=\dfrac13$ so perpendicular gradient $-3$ [M1] $y-3=-3(x-4)$, i.e. $y=-3x+15$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac12\left|1(4-8)+7(8-2)+3(2-4)\right|$ [M1] $=\dfrac12|-4+42-6|=16$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint with gradient the negative reciprocal. The shoelace formula gives the area from coordinates.

subtopic: Finding a coefficient in a binomial expansion
statement: (a) Find the coefficient of $x^3$ in the expansion of $(2x-3)^6$. [4] (b) Find the constant term of $\left(x^2+\dfrac1x\right)^9$. [4]
markscheme: (a) general term $\binom6r(2x)^r(-3)^{6-r}$ [M1] $r=3$ [A1] $\binom63\times2^3\times(-3)^3$ [M1] $=-4320$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) general term $\binom9r\left(x^2\right)^{9-r}\left(x^{-1}\right)^r$ [M1] power of $x$: $18-3r=0$ [A1] $r=6$ [A1] $\binom96=84$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Write the general term, collect the power of $x$, and solve for $r$.

subtopic: Unknown constants from coefficients
statement: In the expansion of $(1+ax)^n$ the coefficient of $x$ is $12$ and the coefficient of $x^2$ is $60$, where $n\in\mathbb Z^+$. (a) Write down two equations in $a$ and $n$. [2] (b) Find $a$ and $n$. [4]
tips: Use the first two coefficients $na$ and $\binom n2a^2$ and eliminate one variable by division or substitution.

subtopic: Binomial expansion with a negative index
statement: Let $f(x)=(1+3x)^{-2}$. (a) Find the first four terms of the expansion of $f(x)$ in ascending powers of $x$. [4] (b) State the range of values of $x$ for which the expansion is valid. [1] (c) Use the first three terms with $x=0.01$ to approximate $\dfrac1{1.03^2}$. [2]
tips: For $(1+u)^n$ with $n$ not a positive integer, use $\binom nr=\dfrac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-r+1)}{r!}$; the series converges for $|u|<1$.

subtopic: Binomial expansion with a fractional index: square root approximation
statement: (a) Expand $(1-4x)^{1/2}$ up to and including the term in $x^3$. [4] (b) Hence approximate $\sqrt{0.96}$ using $x=0.01$, and compare with the calculator value. [3]
tips: Substitute $u=-4x$ into the binomial series for $(1+u)^{1/2}$.

subtopic: Coefficient in a product of expansions
statement: (a) Find the first four terms of the expansion of $(1-x)^5$ in ascending powers of $x$. [2] (b) Hence find the coefficient of $x^3$ in the expansion of $(2+x)(1-x)^5$. [3]
tips: For a product, multiply term by term and collect only those pairs whose powers add to the required power.

subtopic: Sum of binomial coefficients
statement: (a) By putting $x=1$ in the expansion of $(1+x)^n$, show that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk=2^n$. [2] (b) By putting $x=-1$, show that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk=0$ for $n\ge1$. [2] (c) Differentiate $(1+x)^n$ and put $x=1$ to show that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^nk\binom nk=n2^{n-1}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(1+1)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk1^k$ [M1] $=2^n$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $(1-1)^n=0$ [M1] gives the result [A1] [2 marks] (c) $n(1+x)^{n-1}=\sum_{k=1}^nk\binom nkx^{k-1}$ [M1][A1] $x=1$: $n2^{n-1}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Substitute convenient values into a known expansion, or differentiate it first.

subtopic: The greatest term of a binomial expansion
statement: Consider the expansion of $(3+2x)^{10}$ in ascending powers of $x$ with $x=1$. (a) Write down the ratio $\dfrac{T_{r+1}}{T_r}$ of consecutive terms where $T_r=\binom{10}r3^{10-r}2^r$. [3] (b) Find the value of $r$ for which the term is greatest, and the greatest term. [3] (c) Verify using your calculator's table of the terms. [1]
tips: Terms increase while the ratio of consecutive terms exceeds $1$.

subtopic: Using the binomial theorem to approximate a power
statement: (a) Use the first four terms of the expansion of $(1+0.02)^{10}$ to approximate $1.02^{10}$. [3] (b) Find the percentage error compared with the calculator value $1.02^{10}$. [2]
tips: Write the number as $1+h$ with $h$ small so that only the first few terms matter.

subtopic: Binomial expansion after partial fractions
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac1{(1+x)(1-2x)}$ for $|x|<\dfrac12$. (a) Express $f(x)$ in partial fractions. [3] (b) Hence find the expansion of $f(x)$ up to and including the $x^3$ term. [4]
tips: Expand each partial fraction as a geometric/binomial series and add the coefficients.

subtopic: Sum of squares of binomial coefficients
statement: This question proves that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk^2=\binom{2n}n$. (a) Verify the identity for $n=3$. [2] (b) Show that $\binom nk=\binom n{n-k}$. [2] (c) Write $(1+x)^{2n}=(1+x)^n(1+x)^n$. Write down the coefficient of $x^n$ on the left side. [1] (d) By expanding each $(1+x)^n$ on the right side, show that the coefficient of $x^n$ there is $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk\binom n{n-k}$. [3] (e) Hence prove the identity. [2] (f) Use the identity to evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^5\binom5k^2$ and $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{10}\binom{10}k^2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $1+9+9+1=20$ [A1] $\binom63=20$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}$ is symmetric under $k\to n-k$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $\binom{2n}n$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\sum_{i}\binom nix^i\times\sum_j\binom njx^j$ [M1] terms with $i+j=n$ [A1] $\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk\binom n{n-k}$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) equate the coefficients of $x^n$ [M1] use $\binom n{n-k}=\binom nk$ [A1] [2 marks] (f) $\binom{10}5=252$ [A1] $\binom{20}{10}=184756$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Compare coefficients of the same power of $x$ in two different expansions of the same expression.

subtopic: Binomial expansion when the constant is not 1
statement: Let $f(x)=\sqrt{4+x}$. (a) Show that $f(x)=2\left(1+\dfrac x4\right)^{1/2}$ and state the values of $x$ for which the binomial expansion is valid. [3] (b) Find the expansion of $f(x)$ up to and including the $x^3$ term. [4] (c) Use $x=0.2$ to estimate $\sqrt{4.2}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\sqrt{4+x}=\sqrt{4\left(1+\frac x4\right)}$ [M1] $=2\left(1+\dfrac x4\right)^{1/2}$ [A1] valid for $\left|\dfrac x4\right|<1$, i.e. $-4<x<4$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $2\left[1+\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac x4-\dfrac18\left(\dfrac x4\right)^2+\dfrac1{16}\left(\dfrac x4\right)^3\right]$ [M1][A1] $=2+\dfrac x4-\dfrac{x^2}{64}+\dfrac{x^3}{512}$ [A1][A1] [4 marks] (c) $2+0.05-0.000625+0.0000156$ [M1] $=2.049391$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Factor out the constant so the expression has the form $(1+u)^n$ before using the binomial series.
